depthFirst.comment:
Depth first search of a graph generated by a function
`f : α → m α`.

Here `m` must be an `Alternative` `Monad`,
and perhaps the only sensible values are `List` and `MLList MetaM`.

The option `maxDepth` limits the search depth.

Note that if the graph is not a tree then elements will be visited multiple times.
(See `depthFirstRemovingDuplicates`)

explanatories.Option.none: The representation of the absence of a value in the context of an optional type.
explanatories.Option.some: The representation of a present value within an optional type.

depthFirst.fullDefinition: def depthFirst (f : α → m α) (a : α) (maxDepth : Option Nat := none) : m α :=   match maxDepth with   | some d => depthFirst' (fun n a => if n ≤ d then f a else failure) 0 a   | none => depthFirst' (fun _ a => f a) 0 a
depthFirst.description: There is no mathematical statement or concept to summarize as no input was provided.

depthFirstRemovingDuplicates.comment:
Variant of `depthFirst`,
using an internal `HashSet` to record and avoid already visited nodes.

This version describes the graph using `α → MLList m α`,
and returns the monadic lazy list of nodes visited in order.

This is potentially very expensive.
If you want to do efficient enumerations from a generation function,
avoiding duplication up to equality or isomorphism,
use Brendan McKay's method of "generation by canonical construction path".

explanatories.Pure.pure: A function that encapsulates a value within a monadic context, effectively creating an action that returns that value without any additional computation.
explanatories.Option.none: The representation of the absence of a value in the context of an optional type.
explanatories.Alternative.failure: A function that generates an empty collection or signifies a recoverable failure in an alternative computational context.
explanatories.Lean.HashSet: A type that represents a hash set of elements with a specified type and hashing requirements.
explanatories.MonadState.get: A mechanism that retrieves the state from a monadic context.
explanatories.Lean.HashSet.contains: A function that checks whether a specific element is present in a hash set of a defined type, given the necessary equality and hashing conditions.
explanatories.MonadStateOf.set: A function that updates the state in a monadic context to a new specified value.
explanatories.Lean.HashSet.insert: A function that adds a specific element to a hash set of a defined type, given the necessary equality and hashing conditions.

depthFirstRemovingDuplicates.fullDefinition: def depthFirstRemovingDuplicates {α : Type u} [BEq α] [Hashable α]     (f : α → MLList m α) (a : α) (maxDepth : Option Nat := none) : MLList m α := let f' : α → MLList (StateT.{u} (HashSet α) m) α := fun a =>   (f a).liftM >>= fun b => do     let s ← get     if s.contains b then failure     set <| s.insert b     pure b (depthFirst f' a maxDepth).runState' (HashSet.empty.insert a)

Split a lazy list into contiguous sublists,
starting a new sublist each time a monadic predicate changes from `false` to `true`.

explanatories.List.nil: The statement defines the empty list, which is a list type that contains no elements.
explanatories.ULift.down: This definition describes a function that retrieves the underlying value from a lifted type.
explanatories.List.cons: This creates a new list by adding a specified element to the front of an existing list.

MLList.splitAtBecomesTrueM.fullDefinition: partial def splitAtBecomesTrueM (L : MLList m α) (p : α → m (ULift Bool)) : MLList m (List α) :=   aux (L.groupByM p) where aux (M : MLList m (ULift.{u} Bool × List α)) : MLList m (List α) :=   M.cases (fun _ => nil) fun (b, l) t => (if b.down then     t.cases (fun _ => cons l nil)       fun (_, l') t' => cons (l ++ l') (aux t')   else     cons l (aux t))
MLList.splitAtBecomesTrueM.description: This defines a procedure that divides a lazy list into consecutive sublists based on a monadic predicate that indicates transitions from one state to another.

impl.fullDefinition: def impl (maxSize : Option Nat) (f : α → MLList m α) (a : α) : MLList m α :=   let init : BestFirstQueue prio ε m α maxSize := RBMap.single ⟨a, ⊥⟩ (f a)   cons a (iterate go |>.runState' init) where   /-- A single step of the best first search.   Pop an element, and insert its children back into the queue,   with a trivial estimator for their priority. -/   go : StateT (BestFirstQueue prio ε m α maxSize) m α := fun s => do   match ← s.pop with     | none => failure     | some ((_, b), s') => pure (b, s'.insertAndEject ⟨b, ⊥⟩ (f b))
impl.description: This describes the core function of a best-first search algorithm that operates by repeatedly updating a priority queue and processing elements from it to explore their children in a structured manner.

bestFirstSearchCore.code:
bestFirstSearchCore.{u_1} {ω : Type u_1} {α : Type} (prio : α → Thunk ω) (ε : α → Type) [LinearOrder ω]
  [(a : α) → Estimator (prio a) (ε a)] [I : ∀ (a : α), WellFoundedGT ↑(range (bound (prio a)))] [Ord ω] [Ord α]
  {m : Type → Type} [Monad m] [Alternative m] [(a : α) → Bot (ε a)] (f : α → MLList m α) (a : α) (β : Type) [Ord β]
  (removeDuplicatesBy? : Option (α → β) := none) (maxQueued maxDepth : Option ℕ := none) : MLList m α
bestFirstSearchCore.comment:
A lazy list recording the best first search of a graph generated by a function
`f : α → MLList m α`.

We maintain a priority queue of visited-but-not-exhausted nodes,
and at each step take the next child of the highest priority node in the queue.

The option `maxDepth` limits the search depth.

The option `maxQueued` bounds the size of the priority queue,
discarding the lowest priority nodes as needed.
This implements a "beam" search, which may be incomplete but uses bounded memory.

The option `removeDuplicates` keeps an `RBSet` of previously visited nodes.
Otherwise, if the graph is not a tree then nodes will be visited multiple times.

This version allows specifying a custom priority function `prio : α → Thunk ω`
along with estimators `ε : α → Type` equipped with `[∀ a, Estimator (prio a) (ε a)]`
that control the behaviour of the priority queue.
This function returns values `a : α` that have
the lowest possible `prio a` amongst unvisited neighbours of visited nodes,
but lazily estimates these priorities to avoid unnecessary computations.

explanatories.Int.gcd: This definition computes the greatest common divisor of two integers and returns it as a natural number.

Rat.num_mk.description: This theorem states that the numerator of a rational number formed from two integers is equal to the product of the sign of the denominator, the numerator, and the reciprocal of the greatest common divisor of the two integers.

Rat.den_mk.code: Rat.den_mk (n d : ℤ) : (n /. d).den = if d = 0 then 1 else d.natAbs / n.gcd d

explanatories.Int.natAbs: The absolute value of an integer is a natural number representing its non-negative magnitude.

Rat.add_den_dvd.code: Rat.add_den_dvd (q₁ q₂ : ℚ) : (q₁ + q₂).den ∣ q₁.den * q₂.den

Rat.mul_den_dvd.description: This theorem states that the denominator of the product of two rational numbers divides the product of their denominators.

Rat.mul_num.code: Rat.mul_num (q₁ q₂ : ℚ) : (q₁ * q₂).num = q₁.num * q₂.num / ↑((q₁.num * q₂.num).natAbs.gcd (q₁.den * q₂.den))

explanatories.Int.gcd: This definition computes the greatest common divisor of two integers and returns it as a natural number.
explanatories.Nat.gcd: The greatest common divisor function for natural numbers determines the largest natural number that divides both of its inputs.

Rat.mul_num.description: This theorem states that the numerator of the product of two rational numbers is equal to the product of their numerators divided by the greatest common divisor of the absolute values of their product denominators.

Rat.mul_den.code: Rat.mul_den (q₁ q₂ : ℚ) : (q₁ * q₂).den = q₁.den * q₂.den / (q₁.num * q₂.num).natAbs.gcd (q₁.den * q₂.den)

explanatories.Int.gcd: This definition computes the greatest common divisor of two integers and returns it as a natural number.
explanatories.Nat.gcd: The greatest common divisor function for natural numbers determines the largest natural number that divides both of its inputs.

Rat.mul_den.description: This theorem states that the denominator of the product of two rational numbers is equal to the product of their denominators divided by the greatest common divisor of the absolute values of their numerators and the product of their denominators.

Rat.mul_self_num.description: This theorem states that the numerator of the product of a rational number with itself is equal to the square of its numerator.

Rat.mul_self_den.description: This theorem states that the denominator of the square of a rational number is equal to the square of its denominator.

Rat.add_num_den.code: Rat.add_num_den (q r : ℚ) : q + r = (q.num * ↑r.den + ↑q.den * r.num) /. (↑q.den * ↑r.den)
Rat.add_num_den.description: This theorem expresses that the sum of two rational numbers can be computed by combining their numerators and denominators in a specific fractional form.

Rat.isSquare_iff.code: Rat.isSquare_iff {q : ℚ} : IsSquare q ↔ IsSquare q.num ∧ IsSquare q.den

explanatories.IsSquare: An element of a multiplicative type is considered a perfect square if it can be expressed as the product of some element with itself.

Rat.isSquare_iff.description: This theorem states that a rational number is a perfect square if and only if both its numerator and denominator are perfect squares.

explanatories.IsSquare: An element of a multiplicative type is considered a perfect square if it can be expressed as the product of some element with itself.
explanatories.Int.isSquare_natCast_iff: A natural number is a perfect square if and only if its natural casting to integers is also a perfect square.

Rat.isSquare_natCast_iff.description: This theorem states that a natural number is a perfect square if and only if its corresponding integer representation is also a perfect square.

Rat.exists_eq_mul_div_num_and_eq_mul_div.code:
Rat.exists_eq_mul_div_num_and_eq_mul_div_den (n : ℤ) {d : ℤ} (d_ne_zero : d ≠ 0) :
  ∃ c, n = c * (↑n / ↑d).num ∧ d = c * ↑(↑n / ↑d).den
Rat.exists_eq_mul_div_num_and_eq_mul_div.description: This theorem states that for any integer and a non-zero integer, there exists a constant such that the integer can be expressed as the product of this constant and the numerator of the rational number formed by dividing the integer by the non-zero integer, while the non-zero integer can similarly be expressed in terms of its denominator.

Rat.mul_num_den'.code: Rat.mul_num_den' (q r : ℚ) : (q * r).num * ↑q.den * ↑r.den = q.num * r.num * ↑(q * r).den
Rat.mul_num_den'.description: This theorem demonstrates that the product of two rational numbers, when expressed in a specific form, involves a relationship between their numerators and denominators.

Rat.add_num_den'.code: Rat.add_num_den' (q r : ℚ) : (q + r).num * ↑q.den * ↑r.den = (q.num * ↑r.den + r.num * ↑q.den) * ↑(q + r).den
Rat.add_num_den'.description: This theorem expresses that the numerator of the sum of two rational numbers, when written in a specific form, is related to the sum of their numerators adjusted by their denominators.

Rat.substr_num_den'.code: Rat.substr_num_den' (q r : ℚ) : (q - r).num * ↑q.den * ↑r.den = (q.num * ↑r.den - r.num * ↑q.den) * ↑(q - r).den
Rat.substr_num_den'.description: This theorem illustrates that the numerator of the difference between two rational numbers, when expressed in a specific form, is related to their numerators and denominators in a particular equation.

Rat.inv_neg.description: This theorem states that the inverse of a negative rational number is equal to the negative of the inverse of that rational number.

Rat.num_div_eq_of_coprime.code: Rat.num_div_eq_of_coprime {a b : ℤ} (hb0 : 0 < b) (h : a.natAbs.Coprime b.natAbs) : (↑a / ↑b).num = a
Rat.num_div_eq_of_coprime.description: This theorem states that if a positive integer and another integer are coprime, then the numerator of the rational number formed by dividing the integer by the positive integer is equal to the integer itself.

Rat.den_div_eq_of_coprime.code: Rat.den_div_eq_of_coprime {a b : ℤ} (hb0 : 0 < b) (h : a.natAbs.Coprime b.natAbs) : ↑(↑a / ↑b).den = b
Rat.den_div_eq_of_coprime.description: This theorem states that if two integers are coprime, then the denominator of their rational division is equal to the absolute value of the denominator.

Rat.div_int_inj.code:
Rat.div_int_inj {a b c d : ℤ} (hb0 : 0 < b) (hd0 : 0 < d) (h1 : a.natAbs.Coprime b.natAbs)
  (h2 : c.natAbs.Coprime d.natAbs) (h : ↑a / ↑b = ↑c / ↑d) : a = c ∧ b = d
Rat.div_int_inj.description: This theorem states that if two fractions of integers are equal and their numerators are coprime to their respective denominators, then their numerators and denominators must be the same.

Rat.intCast_div_self.description: This theorem states that for any non-zero integer, the division of the integer by itself is equal to the division of its casted values in the rational number system.

Rat.natCast_div_self.description: This theorem states that for any natural number, the quotient of the number by itself is equal to the same number expressed as a rational fraction divided by itself.

Rat.intCast_div.code: Rat.intCast_div (a b : ℤ) (h : b ∣ a) : ↑(a / b) = ↑a / ↑b
Rat.intCast_div.description: This theorem establishes that when an integer divides another integer, the integer division can be expressed as the ratio of their corresponding integer casts.

Rat.natCast_div.code: Rat.natCast_div (a b : ℕ) (h : b ∣ a) : ↑(a / b) = ↑a / ↑b
Rat.natCast_div.description: This theorem states that if an integer is divisible by another, the quotient can be expressed as the ratio of their natural number representations.

Rat.den_div_intCast_eq_one_iff.code: Rat.den_div_intCast_eq_one_iff (m n : ℤ) (hn : n ≠ 0) : (↑m / ↑n).den = 1 ↔ n ∣ m
Rat.den_div_intCast_eq_one_iff.description: This theorem states that the denominator of a rational number formed by dividing one integer by another is equal to one if and only if the second integer divides the first integer.

Rat.ofInt.eq_1.code: Rat.ofInt.eq_1 (num : ℤ) : ofInt num = { num := num, den := 1, den_nz := ofInt.proof_1, reduced := ⋯ }
Rat.ofInt.eq_1.description: This theorem asserts that converting an integer to a rational number results in a fraction with the integer as the numerator and one as the denominator, along with a proof that this fraction is in simplest form.

Rat.inv_intCast_num_of_pos.description: This theorem asserts that the numerator of the multiplicative inverse of a positive integer, when expressed as a rational number, is always one.

Rat.inv_natCast_num_of_pos.description: This theorem asserts that the numerator of the inverse of a positive natural number expressed as a rational number is equal to one.

Rat.inv_intCast_den_of_pos.description: This theorem establishes that for any positive integer expressed as a rational number, the denominator of its inverse is equal to the original integer itself.

Rat.inv_natCast_den_of_pos.description: This theorem establishes that for any positive natural number represented as a rational number, the denominator of its inverse is equal to the original natural number itself.

Rat.inv_intCast_num.description: This theorem asserts that the numerator of the inverse of an integer, when treated as a rational number, is equal to the sign of that integer.

Rat.inv_natCast_num.description: This theorem asserts that for any natural number represented as a rational number, the numerator of its inverse is equal to the sign of the original natural number.

Rat.inv_intCast_den.code: Rat.inv_intCast_den (a : ℤ) : (↑a)⁻¹.den = if a = 0 then 1 else a.natAbs
Rat.inv_intCast_den.description: This theorem asserts that the denominator of the inverse of a casted integer is one if the integer is zero and the absolute value of the integer otherwise.

Rat.inv_natCast_den.code: Rat.inv_natCast_den (a : ℕ) : (↑a)⁻¹.den = if a = 0 then 1 else a
Rat.inv_natCast_den.description: This theorem asserts that the denominator of the inverse of a natural number, when treated as a rational number, is 1 if the natural number is zero and is the natural number itself otherwise.

Rat.forall.code: Rat.forall {p : ℚ → Prop} : (∀ (r : ℚ), p r) ↔ ∀ (a b : ℤ), p (↑a / ↑b)
Rat.forall.description: This theorem establishes that a property holds for all rational numbers if and only if it holds for all pairs of integers used to form those rational numbers through division.

Rat.exists.code: Rat.exists {p : ℚ → Prop} : (∃ r, p r) ↔ ∃ a b, p (↑a / ↑b)
Rat.exists.description: This theorem asserts that the existence of a rational number satisfying a property is equivalent to the existence of two integers such that the rational number formed by their ratio satisfies the same property.

Rat.pnatDen_one.description: This theorem states that the denominator of the rational number one is equal to one.

Rat.pnatDen_zero.description: This theorem establishes that the denominator of zero in the context of positive natural numbers is defined to be one.

Square root function on rational numbers, defined by taking the (integer) square root of the
numerator and the square root (on natural numbers) of the denominator.

Rat.cast_sub_of_ne_zero.code:

Rat.cast_mul_of_ne_zero.{u_3} {α : Type u_3} [DivisionRing α] {p q : ℚ} (hp : ↑p.den ≠ 0) (hq : ↑q.den ≠ 0) :

MonoidHom.apply_mnat.description: This theorem states that the evaluation of a multiplicative homomorphism at a multiplicative natural number can be expressed in terms of its value at one, raised to the power corresponding to the additive representation of that number.

MonoidHom.ext_mnat.code: MonoidHom.ext_mnat.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [Monoid α] ⦃f g : Multiplicative ℕ →* α⦄ (h : f (ofAdd 1) = g (ofAdd 1)) : f = g
MonoidHom.ext_mnat.description: This theorem states that two homomorphisms from the multiplicative natural numbers to a monoid are equal if they produce the same result for the additive equivalent of one.

AddMonoidHom.apply_nat.code: AddMonoidHom.apply_nat.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoid α] (f : ℕ →+ α) (n : ℕ) : f n = n • f 1
AddMonoidHom.apply_nat.description: This theorem states that the value of an additive homomorphism from the natural numbers at a natural number is equivalent to the scalar multiplication of that number by the value of the homomorphism at one.

multiplesAddHom.code: multiplesAddHom.{u_1} (α : Type u_1) [AddCommMonoid α] : α ≃+ (ℕ →+ α)
multiplesAddHom.comment: If `α` is commutative, `multiplesHom` is an additive equivalence.

explanatories.multiplesHom: This definition establishes a bijection between an additive monoid and the additive homomorphisms from natural numbers to that monoid, determined by the image of one.

multiplesAddHom.fullDefinition: def multiplesAddHom : α ≃+ (ℕ →+ α) :=   { multiplesHom α with map_add' := fun a b ↦ AddMonoidHom.ext fun n ↦ by simp [nsmul_add] }
multiplesAddHom.description: This definition describes a structure that establishes an additive equivalence between a commutative additive monoid and the group of additive homomorphisms from the natural numbers to that monoid.

powersMulHom.code: powersMulHom.{u_1} (α : Type u_1) [CommMonoid α] : α ≃* (Multiplicative ℕ →* α)
powersMulHom.comment: If `α` is commutative, `powersHom` is a multiplicative equivalence.

explanatories.powersHom: This definition reveals an equivalence between a monoid and the set of monoid homomorphisms from the natural numbers under multiplication, characterized by their action on the element representing one.

powersMulHom.fullDefinition: def powersMulHom : α ≃* (Multiplicative ℕ →* α) :=   { powersHom α with map_mul' := fun a b ↦ MonoidHom.ext fun n ↦ by simp [mul_pow] }
powersMulHom.description: This definition establishes a multiplicative equivalence between a commutative monoid and the set of multiplicative homomorphisms from the natural numbers to that monoid.

multiplesAddHom_apply.code: multiplesAddHom_apply.{u_1} (α : Type u_1) [AddCommMonoid α] (x : α) (n : ℕ) : ((multiplesAddHom α) x) n = n • x
multiplesAddHom_apply.description: This theorem states that applying the multiples additive homomorphism to an element and a natural number results in the natural number multiplied by that element in an additive commutative monoid.

powersMulHom_apply.code:
powersMulHom_apply.{u_1} (α : Type u_1) [CommMonoid α] (x : α) (n : Multiplicative ℕ) :
  ((powersMulHom α) x) n = x ^ toAdd n
powersMulHom_apply.description: This theorem expresses that for an element in a commutative monoid, the application of a homomorphism derived from powers corresponds to raising that element to the power represented by the associated additive number.

multiplesAddHom_symm_apply.code: multiplesAddHom_symm_apply.{u_1} (α : Type u_1) [AddCommMonoid α] (f : ℕ →+ α) : (multiplesAddHom α).symm f = f 1
multiplesAddHom_symm_apply.description: This theorem asserts that for any additive homomorphism from natural numbers to an additive commutative monoid, the inverse of the multiples homomorphism evaluated at that homomorphism yields the value of the homomorphism at one.

powersMulHom_symm_apply.code:
powersMulHom_symm_apply.{u_1} (α : Type u_1) [CommMonoid α] (f : Multiplicative ℕ →* α) :
  (powersMulHom α).symm f = f (ofAdd 1)
powersMulHom_symm_apply.description: This theorem states that applying the inverse of the homomorphism from natural numbers to a commutative monoid to a multiplicative homomorphism yields the value of that homomorphism at the additive identity of one.

Pi.natCast_apply.code: Pi.natCast_apply.{u_1, u_3} {α : Type u_1} {π : α → Type u_3} [(a : α) → NatCast (π a)] (n : ℕ) (a : α) : ↑n a = ↑n
Pi.natCast_apply.description: This theorem states that for any type indexed by a natural number and a corresponding natural number cast on that type, the result of applying the cast to the natural number with the type index is equivalent to applying the cast to the natural number directly.

Pi.natCast_def.code: Pi.natCast_def.{u_1, u_3} {α : Type u_1} {π : α → Type u_3} [(a : α) → NatCast (π a)] (n : ℕ) : ↑n = fun x => ↑n
Pi.natCast_def.description: This theorem states that for any type that has a natural number cast defined for each element, the casting of a natural number results in a function that returns that number for any input.

Sum.elim_natCast_natCast.code:
Sum.elim_natCast_natCast.{u_3, u_4, u_5} {α : Type u_3} {β : Type u_4} {γ : Type u_5} [NatCast γ] (n : ℕ) :
  Sum.elim ↑n ↑n = ↑n
Sum.elim_natCast_natCast.description: This theorem demonstrates that applying the elimination of a sum to the natural number representation of a sum of natural numbers yields the original natural number itself.

Nat.cast_div.code: Nat.cast_div.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [DivisionSemiring α] {m n : ℕ} (n_dvd : n ∣ m) (hn : ↑n ≠ 0) : ↑(m / n) = ↑m / ↑n

explanatories.Dvd.dvd: The divisibility relation indicates that one element is said to divide another if there exists a third element such that the second element equals the product of the first element and the third element.

Nat.cast_div.description: The theorem establishes that when a natural number divides another natural number and is non-zero, the division of the two natural numbers can be expressed as the division of their corresponding casted values in a division semiring.

Nat.cast_div_div_div_cancel_right.code:
Nat.cast_div_div_div_cancel_right.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [DivisionSemiring α] [CharZero α] {m n d : ℕ} (hn : d ∣ n)
  (hm : d ∣ m) : ↑(m / d) / ↑(n / d) = ↑m / ↑n
Nat.cast_div_div_div_cancel_right.description: The theorem demonstrates that if two natural numbers are divisible by a common natural divisor, the division of the ratios of these numbers can be expressed as the ratio of their corresponding casted values in a division semiring.

Nat.mono_cast.code:
Nat.mono_cast.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] : Monotone Nat.cast
Nat.mono_cast.description: The theorem establishes that the natural number casting function is monotone when applied to types equipped with an additive monoid, a partial order, and certain properties related to zero and one.

Nat.cast_nonneg'.code:
Nat.cast_nonneg'.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] (n : ℕ) : 0 ≤ ↑n
Nat.cast_nonneg'.description: This theorem proves that the natural number cast of any non-negative integer is also non-negative in types that satisfy certain algebraic and order properties.

Nat.cast_add_one_pos.code:
Nat.cast_add_one_pos.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] [NeZero 1] (n : ℕ) : 0 < ↑n + 1
Nat.cast_add_one_pos.description: This theorem demonstrates that the natural number cast of any non-negative integer, when increased by one, remains positive in types that satisfy specific algebraic and order properties.

Nat.strictMono_cast.code:
Nat.strictMono_cast.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] [CharZero α] : StrictMono Nat.cast
Nat.strictMono_cast.description: The theorem establishes that the natural number casting function is strictly monotone in types equipped with an additive monoid, a partial order, and certain properties concerning zero and characteristic zero.

Nat.castOrderEmbedding.code:
Nat.castOrderEmbedding.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] [CharZero α] : ℕ ↪o α

explanatories.Nat.strictMono_cast: The theorem establishes that the natural number casting function is strictly monotone in types equipped with an additive monoid, a partial order, and certain properties concerning zero and characteristic zero.

Nat.castOrderEmbedding.fullDefinition: def castOrderEmbedding : ℕ ↪o α :=   OrderEmbedding.ofStrictMono Nat.cast Nat.strictMono_cast
Nat.castOrderEmbedding.description: This definition describes the natural number casting function as an order embedding into types that possess specific additive, order, and characteristic properties.

Nat.castOrderEmbedding_apply.code:
Nat.castOrderEmbedding_apply.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] [CharZero α] :
  ⇑castOrderEmbedding = Nat.cast
Nat.castOrderEmbedding_apply.description: This theorem shows that the natural number casting function is equivalent to the application of the order embedding defined for natural numbers in types with specific algebraic and order properties.

Nat.cast_le.code:
Nat.cast_le.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] [CharZero α] {m n : ℕ} :
  ↑m ≤ ↑n ↔ m ≤ n
Nat.cast_le.description: This theorem establishes that the natural number cast preserves order by indicating that the cast of two natural numbers is less than or equal to each other if and only if the original numbers are also less than or equal to each other in the context of certain algebraic and ordering properties.

Nat.cast_lt.code:
Nat.cast_lt.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] [CharZero α] {m n : ℕ} :
  ↑m < ↑n ↔ m < n
Nat.cast_lt.description: This theorem asserts that the inequality between natural numbers is preserved under the casting function to certain algebraic types with specified properties.

Nat.one_lt_cast.code:
Nat.one_lt_cast.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] [CharZero α] {n : ℕ} :
  1 < ↑n ↔ 1 < n
Nat.one_lt_cast.description: This theorem establishes that the inequality of one being less than the natural number cast of a positive integer is equivalent to the inequality of one being less than that integer itself in certain algebraic types with specified properties.

Nat.one_le_cast.code:
Nat.one_le_cast.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] [CharZero α] {n : ℕ} :
  1 ≤ ↑n ↔ 1 ≤ n
Nat.one_le_cast.description: This theorem demonstrates that the inequality involving one and the cast of a natural number holds true if and only if the same inequality holds for the original natural number.

Nat.cast_lt_one.code:
Nat.cast_lt_one.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] [CharZero α] {n : ℕ} :
  ↑n < 1 ↔ n = 0
Nat.cast_lt_one.description: This theorem states that the cast of a natural number is less than one if and only if the original natural number is zero, under certain algebraic and order assumptions.

Nat.cast_le_one.code:
Nat.cast_le_one.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [AddMonoidWithOne α] [PartialOrder α]
  [CovariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] [ZeroLEOneClass α] [CharZero α] {n : ℕ} :
  ↑n ≤ 1 ↔ n ≤ 1
Nat.cast_le_one.description: This theorem shows that for any natural number, the condition that its cast is less than or equal to one is equivalent to the original number being less than or equal to one within types that meet certain algebraic and order conditions.

explanatories.OfNat.ofNat: The function allows custom behavior for numeric literals by converting natural numbers into a specified type based on the type's implementation.

Nat.not_ofNat_le_one.description: This theorem establishes that for any natural number that is at least two, its cast to a given type cannot be less than or equal to one, provided that the type satisfies certain algebraic and order properties.

NeZero.nat_of_injective.description: This theorem indicates that if a ring homomorphism is injective and the natural number is not zero, then its cast into a certain semiring remains non-zero.

Nat.cast_nonneg.comment: Specialisation of `Nat.cast_nonneg'`, which seems to be easier for Lean to use.
Nat.cast_nonneg.description: This theorem asserts that the cast of any natural number is non-negative in the context of ordered semirings.

Nat.cast_min.code: Nat.cast_min.{u_3} {α : Type u_3} [LinearOrderedSemiring α] {a b : ℕ} : ↑(min a b) = min ↑a ↑b

explanatories.Min.min: The minimum operation determines the smaller of two given values.

Nat.cast_min.description: This theorem states that the cast of the minimum of two natural numbers is equal to the minimum of their respective casts in the context of linear ordered semirings.

Nat.cast_max.code: Nat.cast_max.{u_3} {α : Type u_3} [LinearOrderedSemiring α] {a b : ℕ} : ↑(max a b) = max ↑a ↑b

explanatories.Max.max: The maximum operation identifies the larger of two given values.

Nat.cast_max.description: This theorem establishes that the cast of the maximum of two natural numbers equals the maximum of their individual casts in the context of linear ordered semirings.

Nat.cast_pos.code: Nat.cast_pos.{u_3} {α : Type u_3} [OrderedSemiring α] [Nontrivial α] {n : ℕ} : 0 < ↑n ↔ 0 < n
Nat.cast_pos.comment: Specialisation of `Nat.cast_pos'`, which seems to be easier for Lean to use.
Nat.cast_pos.description: This theorem asserts that a natural number is positive if and only if its cast into an ordered semiring is also positive, under the condition that the semiring is nontrivial.

explanatories.OfNat.ofNat: The function allows custom behavior for numeric literals by converting natural numbers into a specified type based on the type's implementation.

Nat.ofNat_pos'.description: This theorem confirms that for any natural number greater than or equal to two, its cast into a specific type with certain algebraic properties is positive.

Nat.cast_tsub.code:
Nat.cast_tsub.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [CanonicallyOrderedCommSemiring α] [Sub α] [OrderedSub α]
  [ContravariantClass α α (fun x x_1 => x + x_1) fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] (m n : ℕ) : ↑(m - n) = ↑m - ↑n
Nat.cast_tsub.comment:
A version of `Nat.cast_sub` that works for `ℝ≥0` and `ℚ≥0`. Note that this proof doesn't work
for `ℕ∞` and `ℝ≥0∞`, so we use type-specific lemmas for these types.
Nat.cast_tsub.description: This theorem demonstrates that the cast of the difference between two natural numbers equals the difference of their respective casts in the context of canonically ordered commutative semirings.

Nat.abs_cast.description: This theorem states that the absolute value of the cast of a natural number into a linear ordered ring is equal to the cast of that number itself.

Nat.cast_div_le.code: Nat.cast_div_le.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [LinearOrderedSemifield α] {m n : ℕ} : ↑(m / n) ≤ ↑m / ↑n
Nat.cast_div_le.comment: Natural division is always less than division in the field.
Nat.cast_div_le.description: This theorem states that the cast of the division of two natural numbers is less than or equal to the division of their casts in a linear ordered semifield.

Nat.inv_pos_of_nat.description: This theorem establishes that the inverse of a natural number increased by one is always positive in a linear ordered semifield.

Nat.one_div_pos_of_nat.description: This theorem proves that the reciprocal of a natural number increased by one is always positive in a linear ordered semifield.

Nat.one_div_le_one_div.code:
Nat.one_div_le_one_div.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [LinearOrderedSemifield α] {n m : ℕ} (h : n ≤ m) :
  1 / (↑m + 1) ≤ 1 / (↑n + 1)
Nat.one_div_le_one_div.description: This theorem shows that if one natural number is less than or equal to another, then the reciprocal of the second natural number increased by one is less than or equal to the reciprocal of the first natural number increased by one in a linear ordered semifield.

Nat.one_div_lt_one_div.code:
Nat.one_div_lt_one_div.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [LinearOrderedSemifield α] {n m : ℕ} (h : n < m) :
  1 / (↑m + 1) < 1 / (↑n + 1)
Nat.one_div_lt_one_div.description: This theorem demonstrates that if one natural number is strictly less than another, then the reciprocal of the second natural number increased by one is strictly less than the reciprocal of the first natural number increased by one in a linear ordered semifield.

Nat.cast_withTop.description: This theorem asserts that the cast of a natural number to a certain type with an added top element is equal to the cast of that same natural number.

Nat.cast_withBot.description: This theorem states that the cast of a natural number to a certain type with an added bottom element is equal to the cast of that same natural number.

Nat.image_cast_int_Icc.code: Nat.image_cast_int_Icc (a b : ℕ) : Nat.cast '' Icc a b = Icc ↑a ↑b

explanatories.Set.Icc: This definition describes the set of elements that are greater than or equal to one given element and less than or equal to another in a preorder structure, forming a left-closed and right-closed interval.

Nat.image_cast_int_Icc.description: The theorem asserts that the image of a closed interval of natural numbers under the casting function equals the closed interval formed by the corresponding integers.

Nat.image_cast_int_Ico.code: Nat.image_cast_int_Ico (a b : ℕ) : Nat.cast '' Ico a b = Ico ↑a ↑b

explanatories.Set.Ico: This definition describes the set of elements that are greater than or equal to one given element and strictly less than another in a preorder structure, forming a left-closed and right-open interval.

Nat.image_cast_int_Ico.description: The theorem states that the image of an open interval of natural numbers under the casting function equals the open interval formed by the corresponding integers.

explanatories.Nat.lt: The definition establishes the strict less than relation for natural numbers based on the condition that one number is at least one unit less than another.
explanatories.Nat.le_refl: This theorem asserts that any natural number is less than or equal to itself.
explanatories.Nat.le_trans: If one number is less than or equal to a second number, and the second number is less than or equal to a third number, then the first number is less than or equal to the third number.
explanatories.Nat.lt_iff_le_not_le: The less-than relation for natural numbers is equivalent to being less than or equal to and not greater than or equal to.
explanatories.Nat.le_antisymm: The theorem states that if one natural number is less than or equal to another and vice versa, then the two numbers must be equal.
explanatories.Nat.le_total: For any two natural numbers, one of them is less than or equal to the other.
explanatories.inferInstance: Typeclass inference is a mechanism that automatically generates a value of a specified type based on the available typeclass instances.

Nat.instLinearOrder.fullDefinition: instance instLinearOrder : LinearOrder ℕ where   le := Nat.le   le_refl := @Nat.le_refl   le_trans := @Nat.le_trans   le_antisymm := @Nat.le_antisymm   le_total := @Nat.le_total   lt := Nat.lt   lt_iff_le_not_le := @Nat.lt_iff_le_not_le   decidableLT := inferInstance   decidableLE := inferInstance   decidableEq := inferInstance
Nat.instLinearOrder.description: The definition declares that the natural numbers form a linear order structure.

Nat.succ_pos'.description: The theorem asserts that the successor of any natural number is greater than zero.

Nat.succ_inj.code: Nat.succ_inj {a b : ℕ} : a.succ = b.succ ↔ a = b
Nat.succ_inj.description: The theorem states that if the successors of two natural numbers are equal, then the original numbers must also be equal.

Nat.succ_injective.description: The theorem states that the successor function is injective, meaning that different natural numbers will map to different successors.

Nat.succ_ne_succ.code: Nat.succ_ne_succ {m n : ℕ} : m.succ ≠ n.succ ↔ m ≠ n
Nat.succ_ne_succ.description: The theorem states that if the successors of two natural numbers are not equal, then the original numbers must also be different.

Nat.succ_succ_ne_one.description: The theorem asserts that the successor of a successor of any natural number is not equal to one.

explanatories.Nat.succ: The successor function adds one to a natural number.

Nat.one_lt_succ_succ.description: The theorem states that the successor of the successor of any natural number is greater than one.

LT.lt.nat_succ_le.code: LT.lt.nat_succ_le {n m : ℕ} (h : n < m) : n.succ ≤ m
LT.lt.nat_succ_le.description: The theorem establishes that if one natural number is less than another, then the successor of the first number is less than or equal to the second number.

explanatories.Nat.succ: The successor function adds one to a natural number.

Nat.not_succ_lt_self.description: The theorem states that a natural number is never less than its successor.

Nat.succ_le_iff.code: Nat.succ_le_iff {m n : ℕ} : m.succ ≤ n ↔ m < n
Nat.succ_le_iff.description: The theorem establishes a condition under which the successor of one natural number is less than or equal to another natural number, relating it to a simple inequality.

Nat.le_succ_iff.code: Nat.le_succ_iff {m n : ℕ} : m ≤ n.succ ↔ m ≤ n ∨ m = n.succ

explanatories.Nat.succ: The successor function adds one to a natural number.

Nat.le_succ_iff.description: The theorem establishes that a natural number is less than or equal to the successor of another if and only if it is less than or equal to that number or equal to its successor.

Nat.of_le_succ.code: Nat.of_le_succ {m n : ℕ} : m ≤ n.succ → m ≤ n ∨ m = n.succ
Nat.of_le_succ.description: The theorem indicates that if a natural number is less than or equal to the successor of another natural number, then it is either less than or equal to that number or it equals the successor of that number.

Nat.lt_iff_le_pred.code: Nat.lt_iff_le_pred {m n : ℕ} : 0 < n → (m < n ↔ m ≤ n - 1)

explanatories.Nat.pred: The predecessor function on natural numbers defines a value that is one less than the given natural number.

Nat.lt_iff_le_pred.description: The theorem provides a characterization of the relationship between less than and less than or equal to for natural numbers, linking it with the predecessor in the context of a positive second number.

Nat.le_of_pred_lt.code: Nat.le_of_pred_lt {n : ℕ} {m : ℕ} : m.pred < n → m ≤ n

explanatories.Nat.lt: The definition establishes the strict less than relation for natural numbers based on the condition that one number is at least one unit less than another.
explanatories.Nat.pred: The predecessor function on natural numbers defines a value that is one less than the given natural number.

Nat.le_of_pred_lt.description: The theorem establishes that if the predecessor of a natural number is less than another natural number, then the first number is less than or equal to the second.

Nat.lt_iff_add_one_le.code: Nat.lt_iff_add_one_le {m n : ℕ} : m < n ↔ m + 1 ≤ n
Nat.lt_iff_add_one_le.description: The theorem establishes that a natural number is less than another if and only if adding one to it does not exceed the other number.

Nat.lt_one_add_iff.code: Nat.lt_one_add_iff {m n : ℕ} : m < 1 + n ↔ m ≤ n
Nat.lt_one_add_iff.description: The theorem states that a natural number is less than one plus another natural number if and only if it is less than or equal to that second number.

Nat.one_add_le_iff.code: Nat.one_add_le_iff {m n : ℕ} : 1 + m ≤ n ↔ m < n
Nat.one_add_le_iff.description: The theorem states that adding one to a natural number is less than or equal to another natural number if and only if the first number is strictly less than the second.

Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero.description: The theorem states that a natural number is greater than or equal to one if and only if it is not equal to zero.

Nat.one_lt_iff_ne_zero_and_ne_one.description: The theorem states that a natural number is greater than one if and only if it is not equal to zero and not equal to one.

Nat.lt_one_iff.description: The theorem asserts that a natural number is less than one if and only if it is equal to zero.

Nat.one_le_of_lt.code: Nat.one_le_of_lt {a b : ℕ} (h : a < b) : 1 ≤ b

explanatories.Nat.lt: The definition establishes the strict less than relation for natural numbers based on the condition that one number is at least one unit less than another.

Nat.one_le_of_lt.description: The theorem states that if one natural number is less than another, then the second number is greater than or equal to one.

Nat.min_eq_zero_iff.code: Nat.min_eq_zero_iff {m n : ℕ} : min m n = 0 ↔ m = 0 ∨ n = 0

explanatories.Min.min: The minimum operation determines the smaller of two given values.

Nat.min_eq_zero_iff.description: The theorem states that the minimum of two natural numbers is zero if and only if at least one of the numbers is zero.

Nat.max_eq_zero_iff.code: Nat.max_eq_zero_iff {m n : ℕ} : max m n = 0 ↔ m = 0 ∧ n = 0

explanatories.Max.max: The maximum operation identifies the larger of two given values.

Nat.max_eq_zero_iff.description: The theorem states that the maximum of two natural numbers is zero if and only if both numbers are zero.

explanatories.Nat.add: The addition of natural numbers is defined as the operation that combines two non-negative integers to yield another non-negative integer.

Nat.pred_one_add.description: The theorem proves that the predecessor of one added to any natural number is equal to that natural number.

Nat.pred_eq_self_iff.description: The theorem states that the predecessor of a natural number is equal to that number if and only if the number is zero.

Nat.pred_eq_of_eq_succ.code: Nat.pred_eq_of_eq_succ {m n : ℕ} (H : m = n.succ) : m.pred = n

explanatories.Nat.succ: The successor function adds one to a natural number.

Nat.pred_eq_of_eq_succ.description: The theorem establishes that if one natural number is equal to the successor of another, then its predecessor is equal to the latter number.

Nat.pred_eq_succ_iff.code: Nat.pred_eq_succ_iff {m n : ℕ} : n - 1 = m + 1 ↔ n = m + 2
Nat.pred_eq_succ_iff.description: The theorem states that a natural number minus one is equal to another number plus one if and only if the first number is two more than the second number.

Nat.sqrt_pos.description: The theorem states that the square root of a natural number is positive if and only if the original number is positive.

Nat.sqrt_add_eq.code: Nat.sqrt_add_eq {a : ℕ} (n : ℕ) (h : a ≤ n + n) : (n * n + a).sqrt = n
Nat.sqrt_add_eq.description: The theorem asserts that for a non-negative number, if another number does not exceed the sum of it with itself, then the square root of their sum equals the original number.

Nat.sqrt_add_eq'.code: Nat.sqrt_add_eq' {a : ℕ} (n : ℕ) (h : a ≤ n + n) : (n ^ 2 + a).sqrt = n
Nat.sqrt_add_eq'.description: The theorem states that if a natural number is less than or equal to the sum of itself doubled, then the square root of the sum of the square of that number and another natural number equals the original number.

Nat.sqrt_eq.description: The theorem states that the square root of the square of a natural number is equal to that number itself.

Nat.sqrt_eq'.description: The theorem states that the square root of the square of a natural number is equal to the original natural number itself.

explanatories.Nat.succ: The successor function adds one to a natural number.

Nat.sqrt_succ_le_succ_sqrt.description: The theorem indicates that the square root of the successor of a natural number is less than or equal to the successor of the square root of that number.

Nat.exists_mul_self.code: Nat.exists_mul_self (x : ℕ) : (∃ n, n * n = x) ↔ x.sqrt * x.sqrt = x
Nat.exists_mul_self.description: A natural number can be expressed as the square of another natural number if and only if the square of its integer square root equals the original number.

Nat.exists_mul_self'.code: Nat.exists_mul_self' (x : ℕ) : (∃ n, n ^ 2 = x) ↔ x.sqrt ^ 2 = x
Nat.exists_mul_self'.description: A natural number has a square root that is an integer if and only if the square of its integer square root equals the original number.

Nat.sqrt_mul_sqrt_lt_succ.description: The theorem states that the product of the square root of a natural number with itself is less than one more than that number.

Nat.sqrt_mul_sqrt_lt_succ'.description: The theorem states that the square of the square root of a natural number is less than one more than that number.

Nat.succ_le_succ_sqrt.description: The theorem states that the successor of a natural number is less than or equal to the square of its square root increased by one.

Nat.succ_le_succ_sqrt'.description: The theorem demonstrates that for any natural number, the successor of that number is less than or equal to the square of the successor of its integer square root.

Nat.not_exists_sq.code: Nat.not_exists_sq {m n : ℕ} (hl : m * m < n) (hr : n < (m + 1) * (m + 1)) : ¬∃ t, t * t = n
Nat.not_exists_sq.comment: There are no perfect squares strictly between m² and (m+1)²
Nat.not_exists_sq.description: The theorem proves that if a number is strictly between the squares of two consecutive natural numbers, then it cannot be a perfect square.

Nat.not_exists_sq'.code: Nat.not_exists_sq' {m n : ℕ} : m ^ 2 < n → n < (m + 1) ^ 2 → ¬∃ t, t ^ 2 = n
Nat.not_exists_sq'.description: The theorem asserts that if a natural number is bounded above by the square of an incremented number and below by the square of another number, then that number cannot be a perfect square.

Nat.find_eq_iff.code: Nat.find_eq_iff {m : ℕ} {p : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred p] (h : ∃ n, p n) : Nat.find h = m ↔ p m ∧ ∀ (n : ℕ), n < m → ¬p n
Nat.find_eq_iff.description: The theorem states that under certain conditions, finding a natural number that satisfies a property is equivalent to that number satisfying the property itself and being the least such natural number.

Nat.find_lt_iff.code: Nat.find_lt_iff {p : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred p] (h : ∃ n, p n) (n : ℕ) : Nat.find h < n ↔ ∃ m, m < n ∧ p m
Nat.find_lt_iff.description: The theorem establishes a connection between finding a natural number satisfying a property and the existence of a smaller natural number that also meets that property.

Nat.find_le_iff.code: Nat.find_le_iff {p : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred p] (h : ∃ n, p n) (n : ℕ) : Nat.find h ≤ n ↔ ∃ m, m ≤ n ∧ p m
Nat.find_le_iff.description: The theorem states that for a predicate that has a witness, the least number satisfying that predicate is less than or equal to another number if and only if there exists a number less than or equal to that other number which also satisfies the predicate.

Nat.le_find_iff.code: Nat.le_find_iff {p : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred p] (h : ∃ n, p n) (n : ℕ) : n ≤ Nat.find h ↔ ∀ (m : ℕ), m < n → ¬p m
Nat.le_find_iff.description: The theorem states that a natural number is less than or equal to the least natural number satisfying a given property if and only if all smaller natural numbers do not satisfy that property.

Nat.lt_find_iff.code: Nat.lt_find_iff {p : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred p] (h : ∃ n, p n) (n : ℕ) : n < Nat.find h ↔ ∀ (m : ℕ), m ≤ n → ¬p m
Nat.lt_find_iff.description: The theorem establishes a condition linking the position of a natural number relative to the least number satisfying a given property with the non-existence of that property for all smaller natural numbers.

Nat.find_eq_zero.code: Nat.find_eq_zero {p : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred p] (h : ∃ n, p n) : Nat.find h = 0 ↔ p 0
Nat.find_eq_zero.description: The theorem states that if there exists a natural number satisfying a certain property, then the result of a specific function equals zero if and only if that property holds true for zero.

Nat.find_mono.description: The theorem indicates that the concept of divisibility describes a relationship where one number can evenly divide another if there exists a third number that, when multiplied by the first, equals the second.

Nat.find_le.code: Nat.find_le {n : ℕ} {p : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred p] {h : ∃ n, p n} (hn : p n) : Nat.find h ≤ n
Nat.find_le.description: The theorem establishes that if a specific natural number satisfies a property and there exists at least one natural number with that property, then the result of a certain finding operation on that existence is less than or equal to the original number.

Nat.find_comp_succ.description: The assertion is empty, indicating there is no theorem or definition to summarize.

Nat.find_pos.code: Nat.find_pos {p : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred p] (h : ∃ n, p n) : 0 < Nat.find h ↔ ¬p 0
Nat.find_pos.description: The theorem establishes that the positive value obtained from finding a natural number satisfying a given property corresponds to the negation of that property holding for zero.

explanatories.Nat.add: The addition of natural numbers is defined as the operation that combines two non-negative integers to yield another non-negative integer.

Nat.find_add.description: The statement involves no mathematical content as no theorem or definition is provided.

Nat.findGreatest.code: Nat.findGreatest (P : ℕ → Prop) [DecidablePred P] : ℕ → ℕ
Nat.findGreatest.comment:
`Nat.findGreatest P n` is the largest `i ≤ bound` such that `P i` holds, or `0` if no such `i`
exists

explanatories.DecidablePred: A decidable predicate is a type of logical statement for which it can be determined whether the statement is true or false.

Nat.findGreatest.fullDefinition: def findGreatest (P : ℕ → Prop) [DecidablePred P] : ℕ → ℕ   | 0 => 0   | n + 1 => if P (n + 1) then n + 1 else Nat.findGreatest P n
Nat.findGreatest.description: The definition describes a function that determines the largest natural number less than or equal to a specified bound for which a given property holds, returning zero if no such number exists.

Nat.findGreatest_zero.code: Nat.findGreatest_zero {P : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred P] : findGreatest P 0 = 0
Nat.findGreatest_zero.description: The theorem states that if a property is decidable for natural numbers, then the greatest natural number satisfying that property, when starting from zero, is zero itself.

Nat.findGreatest_succ.description: The theorem cannot be determined as there is no content provided.

Nat.findGreatest_eq.code: Nat.findGreatest_eq {P : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred P] {n : ℕ} : P n → findGreatest P n = n
Nat.findGreatest_eq.description: The theorem states that if a property holds for a natural number, then that number is the largest one satisfying the property when determining the greatest such number.

Nat.findGreatest_of_not.description: The theorem is not specified, therefore no statement can be provided.

Nat.findGreatest_eq_iff.description: The input does not provide any information or context to summarize.

Nat.findGreatest_eq_zero_iff.description: The input does not contain any theorem or definition to summarize.

Nat.findGreatest_spec.code: Nat.findGreatest_spec {m : ℕ} {P : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred P] {n : ℕ} (hmb : m ≤ n) (hm : P m) : P (findGreatest P n)
Nat.findGreatest_spec.description: The theorem asserts that if a natural number satisfies a predicate and is less than or equal to another natural number, then the greatest number satisfying that predicate up to the latter also satisfies the same predicate.

Nat.findGreatest_le.code: Nat.findGreatest_le {P : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred P] (n : ℕ) : findGreatest P n ≤ n
Nat.findGreatest_le.description: The theorem establishes that the greatest natural number satisfying a certain property does not exceed the given natural number.

Nat.le_findGreatest.code: Nat.le_findGreatest {m : ℕ} {P : ℕ → Prop} [DecidablePred P] {n : ℕ} (hmb : m ≤ n) (hm : P m) : m ≤ findGreatest P n

explanatories.Nat.findGreatest: The definition describes a function that determines the largest natural number less than or equal to a specified bound for which a given property holds, returning zero if no such number exists.

Nat.le_findGreatest.description: The theorem states that if a natural number is less than or equal to another number and satisfies a specific property, then it is also less than or equal to the greatest number meeting that property up to the second number.

Nat.findGreatest_mono_right.description: The statement asserts that there is no content to summarize as it references no definitions or theorems.

Nat.lt_sub_iff_add_lt'.code: Nat.lt_sub_iff_add_lt' {a b c : ℕ} : a < c - b ↔ b + a < c
Nat.lt_sub_iff_add_lt'.description: The theorem states that a natural number is less than the difference of two other natural numbers if and only if the sum of one of the numbers and the other is less than the third number.

Nat.sub_lt_sub_iff_right.code: Nat.sub_lt_sub_iff_right {a b c : ℕ} (h : c ≤ a) : a - c < b - c ↔ a < b
Nat.sub_lt_sub_iff_right.description: The theorem demonstrates a condition under which subtracting the same non-negative number from two natural numbers preserves the inequality between the original two numbers.

Nat.decidableLoHi.code: Nat.decidableLoHi (lo hi : ℕ) (P : ℕ → Prop) [H : DecidablePred P] : Decidable (∀ (x : ℕ), lo ≤ x → x < hi → P x)

explanatories.Nat.le_add_right: A natural number is less than or equal to the sum of itself and another natural number.
explanatories.DecidablePred: A decidable predicate is a type of logical statement for which it can be determined whether the statement is true or false.
explanatories.decidable_of_iff: This establishes a method to conclude the decidability of one proposition from the decidability of another when the two propositions are equivalent.
explanatories.Nat.lt_sub_iff_add_lt': The theorem states that a natural number is less than the difference of two other natural numbers if and only if the sum of one of the numbers and the other is less than the third number.
explanatories.Nat.sub_lt_sub_iff_right: The theorem demonstrates a condition under which subtracting the same non-negative number from two natural numbers preserves the inequality between the original two numbers.
explanatories.Nat.add_sub_cancel': If a natural number is less than or equal to another natural number, then the sum of the smaller number and the difference between the two numbers equals the larger number.

Nat.decidableLoHi.fullDefinition: instance decidableLoHi (lo hi : ℕ) (P : ℕ → Prop) [H : DecidablePred P] :     Decidable (∀ x, lo ≤ x → x < hi → P x) :=   decidable_of_iff (∀ x < hi - lo, P (lo + x)) $ by     refine ⟨fun al x hl hh ↦ ?_,       fun al x h ↦ al _ (Nat.le_add_right _ _) (Nat.lt_sub_iff_add_lt'.1 h)⟩     have := al (x - lo) ((Nat.sub_lt_sub_iff_right hl).2 hh)     rwa [Nat.add_sub_cancel' hl] at this
Nat.decidableLoHi.description: This definition introduces a method for determining the decidability of a property for all natural numbers within a specified range.

Nat.decidableLoHiLe.code: Nat.decidableLoHiLe (lo hi : ℕ) (P : ℕ → Prop) [DecidablePred P] : Decidable (∀ (x : ℕ), lo ≤ x → x ≤ hi → P x)

explanatories.Nat.lt_succ_iff: A natural number is less than the successor of another number if and only if it is less than or equal to that number.
explanatories.Iff.rfl: It is established that any proposition is logically equivalent to itself.
explanatories.DecidablePred: A decidable predicate is a type of logical statement for which it can be determined whether the statement is true or false.
explanatories.decidable_of_iff: This establishes a method to conclude the decidability of one proposition from the decidability of another when the two propositions are equivalent.
explanatories.forall₂_congr: This indicates that there is no specific theorem, definition, or content provided to summarize.
explanatories.imp_congr: This theorem establishes that if two propositions are equivalent and a third proposition implies one, then it implies the other.

Nat.decidableLoHiLe.fullDefinition: instance decidableLoHiLe (lo hi : ℕ) (P : ℕ → Prop) [DecidablePred P] :     Decidable (∀ x, lo ≤ x → x ≤ hi → P x) :=   decidable_of_iff (∀ x, lo ≤ x → x < hi + 1 → P x) <|     forall₂_congr fun _ _ ↦ imp_congr Nat.lt_succ_iff Iff.rfl
Nat.decidableLoHiLe.description: This definition provides a method for determining the decidability of a property for all natural numbers within a specified inclusive range.

explanatories.Nat.succ: The successor function adds one to a natural number.

Nat.factorial.fullDefinition: def factorial : ℕ → ℕ   | 0 => 1   | succ n => succ n * factorial n
Nat.factorial.description: The definition specifies a function that computes the factorial of a natural number.
