Set.mem_infs.code: Set.mem_infs.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t : Set α} {c : α} : c ∈ s ⊼ t ↔ ∃ a ∈ s, ∃ b ∈ t, a ⊓ b = c
Set.mem_infs.description: This theorem states that an element belongs to the infimum of two sets if and only if it can be expressed as the meet of some elements from each of the two sets.

Set.inf_mem_infs.code: Set.inf_mem_infs.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t : Set α} {a b : α} : a ∈ s → b ∈ t → a ⊓ b ∈ s ⊼ t
Set.inf_mem_infs.description: This theorem states that if two elements belong to two respective sets, then their infimum is a member of the infimum of the union of those sets.

Set.infs_subset.code: Set.infs_subset.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s₁ s₂ t₁ t₂ : Set α} : s₁ ⊆ s₂ → t₁ ⊆ t₂ → s₁ ⊼ t₁ ⊆ s₂ ⊼ t₂
Set.infs_subset.description: This theorem demonstrates that if one set is a subset of another and a second set is also a subset of a different one, then the infimum of the first pair of sets is a subset of the infimum of the second pair of sets.

Set.infs_subset_left.code: Set.infs_subset_left.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t₁ t₂ : Set α} : t₁ ⊆ t₂ → s ⊼ t₁ ⊆ s ⊼ t₂
Set.infs_subset_left.description: This theorem establishes that if one set is a subset of another, then the infimum of a set with the first set will also be a subset of the infimum with the second set.

Set.infs_subset_right.code: Set.infs_subset_right.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s₁ s₂ t : Set α} : s₁ ⊆ s₂ → s₁ ⊼ t ⊆ s₂ ⊼ t
Set.infs_subset_right.description: This theorem states that if one set is a subset of another, then the infimum of that set combined with a third set will also be a subset of the infimum of the second set with the same third set.

Set.image_subset_infs_left.code:
Set.image_subset_infs_left.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t : Set α} {b : α} :
  b ∈ t → (fun a => a ⊓ b) '' s ⊆ s ⊼ t
Set.image_subset_infs_left.description: This theorem states that if an element belongs to a set, then the image of that set under the operation of taking infimum with the element is a subset of the infimum of the union of the two sets.

Set.image_subset_infs_right.code:
Set.image_subset_infs_right.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t : Set α} {a : α} :
  a ∈ s → (fun x => a ⊓ x) '' t ⊆ s ⊼ t
Set.image_subset_infs_right.description: This theorem states that if an element is in one set, then the image of the infimum of that element with another set is contained within the infimum of both sets.

Set.forall_infs_iff.code:
Set.forall_infs_iff.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t : Set α} {p : α → Prop} :
  (∀ c ∈ s ⊼ t, p c) ↔ ∀ a ∈ s, ∀ b ∈ t, p (a ⊓ b)
Set.forall_infs_iff.description: This theorem states that a property holds for all elements in the infimum of two sets if and only if it holds for the meets of every pair of elements taken from each set.

Set.infs_subset_iff.code: Set.infs_subset_iff.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t u : Set α} : s ⊼ t ⊆ u ↔ ∀ a ∈ s, ∀ b ∈ t, a ⊓ b ∈ u
Set.infs_subset_iff.description: This theorem states that the inclusion of the infimum of two sets in a third set is equivalent to the condition that every pair of elements from the first two sets has their infimum contained in the third set.

Set.infs_nonempty.code: Set.infs_nonempty.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t : Set α} : (s ⊼ t).Nonempty ↔ s.Nonempty ∧ t.Nonempty

explanatories.Set.Nonempty: This defines a property that indicates a set is non-empty, providing a convenient notation for use in theorem assumptions.

Set.infs_nonempty.description: This theorem states that the infimum of two sets is nonempty if and only if both sets are nonempty.

Set.Nonempty.infs.code: Set.Nonempty.infs.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t : Set α} : s.Nonempty → t.Nonempty → (s ⊼ t).Nonempty
Set.Nonempty.infs.description: This theorem states that if two sets are nonempty, then their infimum, or greatest lower bound, is also nonempty.

Set.Nonempty.of_infs_left.code: Set.Nonempty.of_infs_left.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t : Set α} : (s ⊼ t).Nonempty → s.Nonempty
Set.Nonempty.of_infs_left.description: This theorem asserts that if the infimum of two sets is non-empty, then at least one of those sets must also be non-empty.

Set.Nonempty.of_infs_right.code: Set.Nonempty.of_infs_right.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t : Set α} : (s ⊼ t).Nonempty → t.Nonempty
Set.Nonempty.of_infs_right.description: This theorem establishes that if the infimum of two sets is non-empty, then at least one of the sets must also be non-empty.

Set.empty_infs.code: Set.empty_infs.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {t : Set α} : ∅ ⊼ t = ∅
Set.empty_infs.description: This theorem states that the infimum of the empty set with any set is equal to the empty set.

Set.infs_empty.code: Set.infs_empty.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s : Set α} : s ⊼ ∅ = ∅
Set.infs_empty.description: This theorem states that the infimum of any set with the empty set is the empty set itself.

Set.infs_eq_empty.code: Set.infs_eq_empty.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t : Set α} : s ⊼ t = ∅ ↔ s = ∅ ∨ t = ∅
Set.infs_eq_empty.description: This theorem states that the infimum of two sets is empty if and only if at least one of the sets is empty.

Set.singleton_infs.code: Set.singleton_infs.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {t : Set α} {a : α} : {a} ⊼ t = (fun b => a ⊓ b) '' t
Set.singleton_infs.description: This theorem asserts that the infimum of a singleton set and another set is equal to the set of infima of the singleton element with each element of the other set.

Set.infs_singleton.code: Set.infs_singleton.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s : Set α} {b : α} : s ⊼ {b} = (fun a => a ⊓ b) '' s
Set.infs_singleton.description: This theorem shows that the infimum of a set with a singleton set is equivalent to the set of infima of all elements in the original set with the singleton element.

Set.singleton_infs_singleton.code: Set.singleton_infs_singleton.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {a b : α} : {a} ⊼ {b} = {a ⊓ b}
Set.singleton_infs_singleton.description: This theorem states that the infimum of two singleton sets is equal to the singleton set containing the infimum of the two elements.

Set.infs_union_left.code: Set.infs_union_left.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s₁ s₂ t : Set α} : (s₁ ∪ s₂) ⊼ t = s₁ ⊼ t ∪ s₂ ⊼ t
Set.infs_union_left.description: This theorem states that the infimum of the union of two sets with a third set is equal to the union of the infimums of each set with the third set.

Set.infs_union_right.code: Set.infs_union_right.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t₁ t₂ : Set α} : s ⊼ (t₁ ∪ t₂) = s ⊼ t₁ ∪ s ⊼ t₂
Set.infs_union_right.description: This theorem states that the infimum of a set with the union of two other sets is equal to the union of the infimums of the first set with each of the two other sets.

Set.infs_inter_subset_left.code: Set.infs_inter_subset_left.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s₁ s₂ t : Set α} : (s₁ ∩ s₂) ⊼ t ⊆ s₁ ⊼ t ∩ s₂ ⊼ t
Set.infs_inter_subset_left.description: This theorem states that the infimum of the intersection of two sets with a third set is a subset of the intersection of the infima of each of the two sets with the third set.

Set.infs_inter_subset_right.code: Set.infs_inter_subset_right.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s t₁ t₂ : Set α} : s ⊼ (t₁ ∩ t₂) ⊆ s ⊼ t₁ ∩ s ⊼ t₂
Set.infs_inter_subset_right.description: This theorem states that the infimum of a set intersecting with two others is a subset of the infimums of each individual set.

Set.subset_infs_self.code: Set.subset_infs_self.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s : Set α} : s ⊆ s ⊼ s
Set.subset_infs_self.description: This theorem states that any set is a subset of its own infimum.

Set.infs_self_subset.code: Set.infs_self_subset.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] {s : Set α} : s ⊼ s ⊆ s ↔ InfClosed s

explanatories.InfClosed: A set is defined as inf-closed if the infimum of any two elements from the set also belongs to the set.

Set.infs_self_subset.description: This theorem states that a set is InfClosed if and only if its infimum with itself is a subset of the set itself.

Set.iUnion_image_inf_left.code: Set.iUnion_image_inf_left.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] (s t : Set α) : ⋃ a ∈ s, (fun x => a ⊓ x) '' t = s ⊼ t
Set.iUnion_image_inf_left.description: This theorem asserts that the union of the images of a set under the infimum operation with elements from another set is equivalent to the infimum of the original set with that second set.

Set.iUnion_image_inf_right.code:
Set.iUnion_image_inf_right.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] (s t : Set α) :
  ⋃ b ∈ t, (fun x => x ⊓ b) '' s = s ⊼ t
Set.iUnion_image_inf_right.description: This theorem states that the image of the infimum of a set over another set is equal to the infimum of the two sets combined.

Set.image_inf_prod.code: Set.image_inf_prod.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] (s t : Set α) : image2 (fun x x_1 => x ⊓ x_1) s t = s ⊼ t

explanatories.Set.image2: The image of a binary function, when applied to two sets, is defined as the resulting set of values obtained by applying the function to all pairs of elements from the sets.
explanatories.Set.Nonempty.image2: If both sets are non-empty, then the image of a binary function applied to those two sets is also non-empty.

Set.image_inf_prod.description: This theorem establishes that the image of the pointwise infimum of two sets is equal to their infimum as sets.

Set.infs_assoc.code: Set.infs_assoc.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] (s t u : Set α) : s ⊼ t ⊼ u = s ⊼ (t ⊼ u)
Set.infs_assoc.description: This theorem states that the infimum operation is associative, meaning that the infimum of three sets can be grouped in any way without affecting the result.

Set.infs_comm.code: Set.infs_comm.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] (s t : Set α) : s ⊼ t = t ⊼ s
Set.infs_comm.description: This theorem states that the infimum operation is commutative, meaning that the infimum of two sets does not depend on the order in which they are considered.

Set.infs_left_comm.code: Set.infs_left_comm.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] (s t u : Set α) : s ⊼ (t ⊼ u) = t ⊼ (s ⊼ u)
Set.infs_left_comm.description: This theorem establishes that the infimum operation is commutative with respect to three sets, meaning the order of the last two does not affect the result.

Set.infs_right_comm.code: Set.infs_right_comm.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] (s t u : Set α) : s ⊼ t ⊼ u = s ⊼ u ⊼ t
Set.infs_right_comm.description: This theorem states that the infimum operation is commutative when applied successively to three sets.

Set.infs_infs_infs_comm.code: Set.infs_infs_infs_comm.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] (s t u v : Set α) : s ⊼ t ⊼ (u ⊼ v) = s ⊼ u ⊼ (t ⊼ v)
Set.infs_infs_infs_comm.description: This theorem states that the infimum operation applied to four sets is commutative regardless of the grouping of the sets.

Set.sups_infs_subset_left.code: Set.sups_infs_subset_left.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [DistribLattice α] (s t u : Set α) : s ⊻ t ⊼ u ⊆ (s ⊻ t) ⊼ (s ⊻ u)
Set.sups_infs_subset_left.description: This theorem asserts that the supremum of a set combined with the infimum of another set and a third set is a subset of the infimum of the combined sets' supremum and the supremum of the third set.

Set.sups_infs_subset_right.code: Set.sups_infs_subset_right.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [DistribLattice α] (s t u : Set α) : t ⊼ u ⊻ s ⊆ (t ⊻ s) ⊼ (u ⊻ s)
Set.sups_infs_subset_right.description: This theorem states that the infimum of one set combined with the supremum of two sets is a subset of the infimum formed by the supremum of the first set with the other.

Set.infs_sups_subset_left.code: Set.infs_sups_subset_left.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [DistribLattice α] (s t u : Set α) : s ⊼ (t ⊻ u) ⊆ s ⊼ t ⊻ s ⊼ u
Set.infs_sups_subset_left.description: This theorem states that the infimum of a set with the union of two other sets is contained within the union of the infimums of the first set with each of the other two sets separately.

Set.infs_sups_subset_right.code: Set.infs_sups_subset_right.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [DistribLattice α] (s t u : Set α) : (t ⊻ u) ⊼ s ⊆ t ⊼ s ⊻ u ⊼ s
Set.infs_sups_subset_right.description: This theorem states that the infimum of the supremum of two sets with a third set is contained within the union of the infimum with the first set and the supremum with the second set.

upperClosure_sups.code:
upperClosure_sups.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeSup α] (s t : Set α) :
  upperClosure (s ⊻ t) = upperClosure s ⊔ upperClosure t

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.

upperClosure_sups.description: This theorem shows that the upper closure of the supremum of two sets is equivalent to the supremum of the upper closures of each set individually.

lowerClosure_infs.code:
lowerClosure_infs.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [SemilatticeInf α] (s t : Set α) :
  lowerClosure (s ⊼ t) = lowerClosure s ⊓ lowerClosure t

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.

lowerClosure_infs.description: This theorem demonstrates that the lower closure of the infimum of two sets is equal to the infimum of the lower closures of each set.

Set.EquitableOn.code: Set.EquitableOn.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} [LE β] [Add β] [One β] (s : Set α) (f : α → β) : Prop
Set.EquitableOn.comment: A set is equitable if no element value is more than one bigger than another.
Set.EquitableOn.fullDefinition: def EquitableOn [LE β] [Add β] [One β] (s : Set α) (f : α → β) : Prop :=   ∀ ⦃a₁ a₂⦄, a₁ ∈ s → a₂ ∈ s → f a₁ ≤ f a₂ + 1
Set.EquitableOn.description: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.

Set.equitableOn_empty.code: Set.equitableOn_empty.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} [LE β] [Add β] [One β] (f : α → β) : ∅.EquitableOn f

explanatories.Set.EquitableOn: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.

Set.equitableOn_empty.description: The empty set is deemed equitable for any function assigning values to its elements.

Set.equitableOn_iff_exists_le_le_add_one.code:
Set.equitableOn_iff_exists_le_le_add_one.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s : Set α} {f : α → ℕ} :
  s.EquitableOn f ↔ ∃ b, ∀ a ∈ s, b ≤ f a ∧ f a ≤ b + 1

explanatories.Set.EquitableOn: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.

Set.equitableOn_iff_exists_le_le_add_one.description: A set is equitable for a function if and only if there exists a bound such that all assigned values to elements of the set are either equal to that bound or one greater.

Set.equitableOn_iff_exists_image_subset_.code:
Set.equitableOn_iff_exists_image_subset_icc.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s : Set α} {f : α → ℕ} :
  s.EquitableOn f ↔ ∃ b, f '' s ⊆ Icc b (b + 1)

explanatories.Set.EquitableOn: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.
explanatories.Set.Icc: This definition describes the set of elements that are greater than or equal to one given element and less than or equal to another in a preorder structure, forming a left-closed and right-closed interval.

Set.equitableOn_iff_exists_image_subset_.description: A set is equitable for a function if and only if there exists a bound such that the image of the set under the function is contained within a closed interval of width two.

Set.equitableOn_iff_exists_eq_eq_add_one.code:
Set.equitableOn_iff_exists_eq_eq_add_one.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s : Set α} {f : α → ℕ} :
  s.EquitableOn f ↔ ∃ b, ∀ a ∈ s, f a = b ∨ f a = b + 1

explanatories.Set.EquitableOn: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.

Set.equitableOn_iff_exists_eq_eq_add_one.description: A set is equitable for a function if and only if there exists a bound such that all assigned values to elements of the set are either equal to that bound or one greater.

Set.Subsingleton.equitableOn.code:
Set.Subsingleton.equitableOn.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} [OrderedSemiring β] {s : Set α}
  (hs : s.Subsingleton) (f : α → β) : s.EquitableOn f

explanatories.Set.EquitableOn: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.

Set.Subsingleton.equitableOn.description: A subsingleton set is equitable for a function if the assigned values to its elements do not vary, meaning they are all the same.

Set.equitableOn_singleton.code:
Set.equitableOn_singleton.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} [OrderedSemiring β] (a : α) (f : α → β) :
  {a}.EquitableOn f

explanatories.Set.EquitableOn: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.

Set.equitableOn_singleton.description: A singleton set is considered equitable for any function assigning values to its elements.

Finset.equitableOn_iff_le_le_add_one.code:
Finset.equitableOn_iff_le_le_add_one.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} {f : α → ℕ} :
  (↑s).EquitableOn f ↔ ∀ a ∈ s, (∑ i ∈ s, f i) / s.card ≤ f a ∧ f a ≤ (∑ i ∈ s, f i) / s.card + 1

explanatories.Set.EquitableOn: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.
explanatories.Finset.card: This definition indicates that the cardinality of a finite set represents the total number of its elements.

Finset.equitableOn_iff_le_le_add_one.description: A finite set is equitable for a function if and only if the value assigned to each element is within one unit of the average of the values assigned to all elements in the set.

Finset.EquitableOn.le.code:
Finset.EquitableOn.le.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} {f : α → ℕ} {a : α} (h : (↑s).EquitableOn f) (ha : a ∈ s) :
  (∑ i ∈ s, f i) / s.card ≤ f a

explanatories.Set.EquitableOn: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.
explanatories.Finset.card: This definition indicates that the cardinality of a finite set represents the total number of its elements.

Finset.EquitableOn.le.description: The sum of values assigned to the elements of a finite set divided by the number of elements is less than or equal to the value assigned to any given element in the set when the set is equitable.

Finset.EquitableOn.le_add_one.code:
Finset.EquitableOn.le_add_one.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} {f : α → ℕ} {a : α} (h : (↑s).EquitableOn f)
  (ha : a ∈ s) : f a ≤ (∑ i ∈ s, f i) / s.card + 1

explanatories.Set.EquitableOn: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.
explanatories.Finset.card: This definition indicates that the cardinality of a finite set represents the total number of its elements.

Finset.EquitableOn.le_add_one.description: If a finite set is equitable with respect to a function assigning natural numbers to its elements, then the value assigned to any element does not exceed the average of all assigned values plus one.

Finset.equitableOn_iff.code:
Finset.equitableOn_iff.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} {f : α → ℕ} :
  (↑s).EquitableOn f ↔ ∀ a ∈ s, f a = (∑ i ∈ s, f i) / s.card ∨ f a = (∑ i ∈ s, f i) / s.card + 1

explanatories.Set.EquitableOn: A set is considered equitable if the values assigned to its elements do not differ by more than one.
explanatories.Finset.card: This definition indicates that the cardinality of a finite set represents the total number of its elements.

Finset.equitableOn_iff.description: A finite set is equitable for a function if and only if each assigned value to its elements is either equal to the average of those values or one unit greater.

Set.mulAntidiagonal.code: Set.mulAntidiagonal.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [Mul α] (s t : Set α) (a : α) : Set (α × α)
Set.mulAntidiagonal.comment:
`Set.mulAntidiagonal s t a` is the set of all pairs of an element in `s` and an element in `t`
that multiply to `a`.
Set.mulAntidiagonal.fullDefinition: def mulAntidiagonal (s t : Set α) (a : α) : Set (α × α) :=   { x | x.1 ∈ s ∧ x.2 ∈ t ∧ x.1 * x.2 = a }
Set.mulAntidiagonal.description: The definition describes a set containing all pairs of elements from two given sets whose product equals a specified value.

set.mul_antidiagonal.code: Set.mulAntidiagonal.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [Mul α] (s t : Set α) (a : α) : Set (α × α)
set.mul_antidiagonal.comment:
`Set.mulAntidiagonal s t a` is the set of all pairs of an element in `s` and an element in `t`
that multiply to `a`.

set.mul_antidiagonal.description: The definition describes a set containing all pairs of elements from two given sets whose product equals a specified value.

set.add_antidiagonal.code: Set.mulAntidiagonal.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [Mul α] (s t : Set α) (a : α) : Set (α × α)
set.add_antidiagonal.comment:
`Set.mulAntidiagonal s t a` is the set of all pairs of an element in `s` and an element in `t`
that multiply to `a`.
set.add_antidiagonal.fullDefinition: def mulAntidiagonal (s t : Set α) (a : α) : Set (α × α) :=   { x | x.1 ∈ s ∧ x.2 ∈ t ∧ x.1 * x.2 = a }
set.add_antidiagonal.description: The definition describes a set containing all pairs of elements from two given sets whose product equals a specified value.

Set.addAntidiagonal.code: Set.mulAntidiagonal.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [Mul α] (s t : Set α) (a : α) : Set (α × α)
Set.addAntidiagonal.comment:
`Set.mulAntidiagonal s t a` is the set of all pairs of an element in `s` and an element in `t`
that multiply to `a`.
Set.addAntidiagonal.fullDefinition: def mulAntidiagonal (s t : Set α) (a : α) : Set (α × α) :=   { x | x.1 ∈ s ∧ x.2 ∈ t ∧ x.1 * x.2 = a }
Set.addAntidiagonal.description: The definition describes a set containing all pairs of elements from two given sets whose product equals a specified value.

Set.mem_mulAntidiagonal.code:
Set.mem_mulAntidiagonal.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [Mul α] {s t : Set α} {a : α} {x : α × α} :
  x ∈ s.mulAntidiagonal t a ↔ x.1 ∈ s ∧ x.2 ∈ t ∧ x.1 * x.2 = a

explanatories.Set.mulAntidiagonal: The definition describes a set containing all pairs of elements from two given sets whose product equals a specified value.

Trunc.comment:
`Trunc α` is the quotient of `α` by the always-true relation. This
is related to the propositional truncation in HoTT, and is similar
in effect to `Nonempty α`, but unlike `Nonempty α`, `Trunc α` is data,
so the VM representation is the same as `α`, and so this can be used to
maintain computability.

PNat.modDivAux.code: PNat.modDivAux : ℕ+ → ℕ → ℕ → ℕ+ × ℕ
PNat.modDivAux.comment:
We define `m % k` and `m / k` in the same way as for `ℕ`
except that when `m = n * k` we take `m % k = k` and
`m / k = n - 1`.  This ensures that `m % k` is always positive
and `m = (m % k) + k * (m / k)` in all cases.  Later we
define a function `div_exact` which gives the usual `m / k`
in the case where `k` divides `m`.

PNat.modDivAux.description: This definition establishes a method for calculating the modulus and division of positive natural numbers, ensuring the results remain positive and conform to specific rules when the number is a multiple of the divisor.

PNat.modDiv.comment:

We define `m % k` and `m / k` in the same way as for `ℕ`

`m / k = n - 1`.  This ensures that `m % k` is always positive

define a function `div_exact` which gives the usual `m / k`
in the case where `k` divides `m`.

explanatories.PNat.modDivAux: This definition establishes a method for calculating the modulus and division of positive natural numbers, ensuring the results remain positive and conform to specific rules when the number is a multiple of the divisor.

PNat.caseStrongInductionOn.fullDefinition: def caseStrongInductionOn {p : ℕ+ → Sort*} (a : ℕ+) (hz : p 1)     (hi : ∀ n, (∀ m, m ≤ n → p m) → p (n + 1)) : p a := by   apply strongInductionOn a   rintro ⟨k, kprop⟩ hk   cases' k with k   · exact (lt_irrefl 0 kprop).elim   cases' k with k   · exact hz   exact hi ⟨k.succ, Nat.succ_pos _⟩ fun m hm => hk _ (Nat.lt_succ_iff.2 hm)
PNat.caseStrongInductionOn.description: This definition provides a strong induction principle for positive natural numbers where the base case is established for one and the inductive step involves proving a property for the successor of each positive natural number.

PNat.recOn.code: PNat.recOn.{u_1} (n : ℕ+) {p : ℕ+ → Sort u_1} (p1 : p 1) (hp : (n : ℕ+) → p n → p (n + 1)) : p n
PNat.recOn.comment:
An induction principle for `ℕ+`: it takes values in `Sort*`, so it applies also to Types,

PNat.recOn.fullDefinition: def recOn (n : ℕ+) {p : ℕ+ → Sort*} (p1 : p 1) (hp : ∀ n, p n → p (n + 1)) : p n := by   rcases n with ⟨n, h⟩   induction' n with n IH   · exact absurd h (by decide)   · cases' n with n     · exact p1     · exact hp _ (IH n.succ_pos)
PNat.recOn.description: This definition introduces an induction principle for positive natural numbers that allows for proofs in various types, not limited to propositions.

PNat.recOn_one.code: PNat.recOn_one.{u_1} {p : ℕ+ → Sort u_1} (p1 : p 1) (hp : (n : ℕ+) → p n → p (n + 1)) : recOn 1 p1 hp = p1
PNat.recOn_one.description: This theorem demonstrates that the recursive function applied to the number one with a base case and a successor step returns the base case itself.

PNat.recOn_succ.code:
PNat.recOn_succ.{u_1} (n : ℕ+) {p : ℕ+ → Sort u_1} (p1 : p 1) (hp : (n : ℕ+) → p n → p (n + 1)) :
  (n + 1).recOn p1 hp = hp n (n.recOn p1 hp)
PNat.recOn_succ.description: This theorem states that the recursive application of a property for positive natural numbers can be expressed in terms of the property at one number and its successor, ensuring consistency in the recursive structure.

PNat.findX.fullDefinition: protected def findX : { n // p n ∧ ∀ m : ℕ+, m < n → ¬p m } := by   have : ∃ (n' : ℕ) (n : ℕ+) (_ : n' = n), p n := Exists.elim h fun n hn => ⟨n, n, rfl, hn⟩   have n := Nat.findX this   refine ⟨⟨n, ?_⟩, ?_, fun m hm pm => ?_⟩   · obtain ⟨n', hn', -⟩ := n.prop.1     rw [hn']     exact n'.prop   · obtain ⟨n', hn', pn'⟩ := n.prop.1     simpa [hn', Subtype.coe_eta] using pn'   · exact n.prop.2 m hm ⟨m, rfl, pm⟩

PNat.find.code: PNat.find {p : ℕ+ → Prop} [DecidablePred p] (h : ∃ n, p n) : ℕ+
PNat.find.comment:
If `p` is a (decidable) predicate on `ℕ+` and `hp : ∃ (n : ℕ+), p n` is a proof that
there exists some positive natural number satisfying `p`, then `PNat.find hp` is the
smallest positive natural number satisfying `p`. Note that `PNat.find` is protected,
meaning that you can't just write `find`, even if the `PNat` namespace is open.

The API for `PNat.find` is:

* `PNat.find_spec` is the proof that `PNat.find hp` satisfies `p`.
* `PNat.find_min` is the proof that if `m < PNat.find hp` then `m` does not satisfy `p`.
* `PNat.find_min'` is the proof that if `m` does satisfy `p` then `PNat.find hp ≤ m`.

PrimeMultiset.comment:
The type of multisets of prime numbers.  Unique factorization
gives an equivalence between this set and ℕ+, as we will formalize
below.

explanatories.Nat.Primes: The type defined here represents the collection of prime numbers.
explanatories.id: The identity function returns its input unchanged and can be used to explicitly assign a type to an expression for typeclass inference purposes.

PrimeMultiset.fullDefinition: def PrimeMultiset :=   Multiset Nat.Primes deriving Inhabited, CanonicallyOrderedAddCommMonoid, DistribLattice,   SemilatticeSup, Sub
PrimeMultiset.description: This definition introduces the type representing multisets of prime numbers, which uniquely relate to positive natural numbers through factorization.

PrimeMultiset.toNatMultiset.comment:
We can forget the primality property and regard a multiset
of primes as just a multiset of positive integers, or a multiset
of natural numbers.  In the opposite direction, if we have a
multiset of positive integers or natural numbers, together with
a proof that all the elements are prime, then we can regard it
as a multiset of primes.  The next block of results records
obvious properties of these coercions.

PNat.factorMultiset_mul.code: PNat.factorMultiset_mul (n m : ℕ+) : (n * m).factorMultiset = n.factorMultiset + m.factorMultiset
PNat.factorMultiset_mul.description: This theorem states that the factorization multiset of the product of two positive natural numbers is the sum of their respective factorization multisets.

PNat.factorMultiset_le_iff.code: PNat.factorMultiset_le_iff {m n : ℕ+} : m.factorMultiset ≤ n.factorMultiset ↔ m ∣ n
PNat.factorMultiset_le_iff.comment:
We now have four different results that all encode the
idea that inequality of multisets corresponds to divisibility
of positive integers.
PNat.factorMultiset_le_iff.description: This theorem indicates that the multiset representation of the prime factorization of one positive integer being less than or equal to that of another is equivalent to the first integer being a divisor of the second.

Matrix.of.code: Matrix.of.{v, u_2, u_3} {m : Type u_2} {n : Type u_3} {α : Type v} : (m → n → α) ≃ Matrix m n α
Matrix.of.comment:
Cast a function into a matrix.

The two sides of the equivalence are definitionally equal types. We want to use an explicit cast
to distinguish the types because `Matrix` has different instances to pi types (such as `Pi.mul`,
which performs elementwise multiplication, vs `Matrix.mul`).

If you are defining a matrix, in terms of its entries, use `of (fun i j ↦ _)`. The
purpose of this approach is to ensure that terms of the form `(fun i j ↦ _) * (fun i j ↦ _)` do not
appear, as the type of `*` can be misleading.

Porting note: In Lean 3, it is also safe to use pattern matching in a definition as `| i j := _`,
which can only be unfolded when fully-applied. leanprover/lean4#2042 means this does not
(currently) work in Lean 4.

explanatories.Equiv.refl: This definition states that every type is self-equivalent, meaning it has an equivalence relation to itself.
explanatories.AddEquiv.refl: The identity map on an additive structure is an additive isomorphism.
explanatories.LinearEquiv.refl: This definition asserts that the identity map can be viewed as a linear equivalence between a module and itself over a semiring.
explanatories.RingEquiv.refl: This defines the identity map as a ring isomorphism for a given ring.
explanatories.AlgEquiv.refl: This definition specifies that there is a reflexive algebraic equivalence for any algebra over a commutative semiring, meaning each algebra is equivalent to itself.

matrix.of.comment:
Cast a function into a matrix.

The two sides of the equivalence are definitionally equal types. We want to use an explicit cast
to distinguish the types because `Matrix` has different instances to pi types (such as `Pi.mul`,
which performs elementwise multiplication, vs `Matrix.mul`).

If you are defining a matrix, in terms of its entries, use `of (fun i j ↦ _)`. The
purpose of this approach is to ensure that terms of the form `(fun i j ↦ _) * (fun i j ↦ _)` do not
appear, as the type of `*` can be misleading.

Porting note: In Lean 3, it is also safe to use pattern matching in a definition as `| i j := _`,
which can only be unfolded when fully-applied. leanprover/lean4#2042 means this does not
(currently) work in Lean 4.

explanatories.Equiv.refl: This definition states that every type is self-equivalent, meaning it has an equivalence relation to itself.
explanatories.AddEquiv.refl: The identity map on an additive structure is an additive isomorphism.
explanatories.LinearEquiv.refl: This definition asserts that the identity map can be viewed as a linear equivalence between a module and itself over a semiring.
explanatories.RingEquiv.refl: This defines the identity map as a ring isomorphism for a given ring.
explanatories.AlgEquiv.refl: This definition specifies that there is a reflexive algebraic equivalence for any algebra over a commutative semiring, meaning each algebra is equivalent to itself.

matrix.of.fullDefinition: def of : (m → n → α) ≃ Matrix m n α :=   Equiv.refl _
matrix.of.description: A function that takes two indices and returns an entry can be equivalently represented as a matrix composed of those entries.

explanatories.Equiv.symm: This definition describes the operation that produces the inverse equivalence relation from a given equivalence relation between two types.
explanatories.Ne.symm: If two elements are not equal to each other, then reversing their order also indicates that they are not equal.
explanatories.Eq.symm: Equality is symmetric, meaning that if one element is equal to another, then the second is equal to the first.
explanatories.AddEquiv.symm: The definition states that the inverse of an additive isomorphism is also an additive isomorphism.
explanatories.LinearEquiv.symm: This definition specifies the symmetry of linear equivalences, indicating that the inverse relationship between two modules can be expressed as a linear equivalence in the opposite direction.
explanatories.RingEquiv.symm: This defines the inverse of a ring isomorphism as another ring isomorphism between the respective rings.
explanatories.AlgEquiv.symm: This definition indicates that every algebra equivalence has a corresponding inverse that switches the roles of the two algebras involved.

Matrix.vecMulVec.comment:
For two vectors `w` and `v`, `vecMulVec w v i j` is defined to be `w i * v j`.
Put another way, `vecMulVec w v` is exactly `col w * row v`.

  (M : Matrix m n α) (v : n → α) : m → α
Matrix.mulVec.comment:
`M *ᵥ v` (notation for `mulVec M v`) is the matrix-vector product of matrix `M` and vector `v`,
where `v` is seen as a column vector.
Put another way, `M *ᵥ v` is the vector whose entries are those of `M * col v` (see `col_mulVec`).

The notation has precedence 73, which comes immediately before ` ⬝ᵥ ` for `Matrix.dotProduct`,
so that `A *ᵥ v ⬝ᵥ B *ᵥ w` is parsed as `(A *ᵥ v) ⬝ᵥ (B *ᵥ w)`.
Matrix.mulVec.fullDefinition: def mulVec [Fintype n] (M : Matrix m n α) (v : n → α) : m → α   | i => (fun j => M i j) ⬝ᵥ v
Matrix.mulVec.description: The matrix-vector product of a matrix and a vector is a function that maps each row of the matrix to the corresponding entry of the resulting vector.

explanatories.DecidableEq: A type is said to have decidable equality if it is possible to determine whether any two elements of that type are equal.
explanatories.MulOpposite.op: This definition specifies a function that maps an element from a type to its corresponding element in the multiplicative opposite type.
explanatories.Matrix.diagonal_transpose: The transpose of a diagonal matrix is equal to the original diagonal matrix.
explanatories.Eq.trans: If one element is equal to a second, and that second is equal to a third, then the first element is also equal to the third, demonstrating the transitive property of equality.
explanatories.Matrix.algebraMap_eq_diagonal: The algebra map from a commutative semiring to the matrix algebra is represented by a diagonal matrix whose entries are determined by another algebra map applied to functions producing vector values.
explanatories.Pi.algebraMap_apply: This theorem demonstrates that applying the algebra map from a commutative semiring to a function space directly yields the same result as applying the algebra map to each individual algebra in that space.
explanatories.Equiv.trans: This definition establishes a method for composing two equivalence relations to create a new equivalence relation between the first and last types.
explanatories.AddEquiv.trans: There is no definition provided to summarize.
explanatories.LinearEquiv.trans: This definition establishes that if there are two linear equivalences between three modules with corresponding ring homomorphisms, then there exists a direct linear equivalence between the first and last modules.
explanatories.RingEquiv.trans: This defines a construction that allows the composition of two ring equivalences to produce a new ring equivalence between the original and the final structures.
explanatories.AlgHom.commutes': This theorem states that for an algebra homomorphism between two algebras over a commutative semiring, applying the ring homomorphism form of the algebra homomorphism to an element mapped from the semiring reproduces the mapping of that element in the target algebra.
explanatories.AlgEquiv.trans: This definition establishes that the composition of two algebra equivalences is itself an algebra equivalence, demonstrating that the property of algebra equivalence is transitive.
explanatories.Iff.trans: If two propositions are each equivalent to a third proposition, then they are equivalent to each other.
explanatories.Equiv.toFun: This definition specifies a function that retrieves the mapping from one type to another represented by an equivalence relation.
explanatories.MulOpposite.opAddEquiv: This definition establishes an additive equivalence between a type and its opposite structure in an additive context.
explanatories.Matrix.transposeRingEquiv: The transpose of a matrix is shown to have an equivalence in the context of ring theory, relating it to the opposite ring of matrices with identical structure.
explanatories.MulOpposite.algebraMap_apply: This theorem demonstrates that applying the algebra map from a commutative semiring to an algebra in its opposite category is equivalent to applying the algebra map in the original category, followed by taking the opposite element.

matrix.transpose_alg_equiv.fullDefinition: def transposeAlgEquiv [CommSemiring R] [CommSemiring α] [Fintype m] [DecidableEq m] [Algebra R α] :     Matrix m m α ≃ₐ[R] (Matrix m m α)ᵐᵒᵖ :=   { (transposeAddEquiv m m α).trans MulOpposite.opAddEquiv,     transposeRingEquiv m α with     toFun := fun M => MulOpposite.op Mᵀ     commutes' := fun r => by       simp only [algebraMap_eq_diagonal, diagonal_transpose, MulOpposite.algebraMap_apply] }
matrix.transpose_alg_equiv.description: The transpose operation on matrices is equivalent to an algebraic isomorphism to the opposite ring of matrices with the same dimensions.

Matrix.submatrix.comment:
Given maps `(r_reindex : l → m)` and `(c_reindex : o → n)` reindexing the rows and columns of
a matrix `M : Matrix m n α`, the matrix `M.submatrix r_reindex c_reindex : Matrix l o α` is defined
by `(M.submatrix r_reindex c_reindex) i j = M (r_reindex i) (c_reindex j)` for `(i,j) : l × o`.
Note that the total number of row and columns does not have to be preserved.

explanatories.TrivSqZeroExt.algebraMap_eq_inl': This theorem demonstrates that the algebra map from a commutative semiring to the trivial square-zero extension is equivalent to the inclusion of the image of the algebra map into the base ring.

explanatories.TrivSqZeroExt.algebraMap_eq_inl: This theorem states that the algebra map from a commutative semiring to its trivial square-zero extension coincides with the inclusion of elements from the semiring.

Matrix.matrixNotation.comment:
Notation for m×n matrices, aka `Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) α`.

For instance:
* `!![a, b, c; d, e, f]` is the matrix with two rows and three columns, of type
  `Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 3) α`
* `!![a, b, c]` is a row vector of type `Matrix (Fin 1) (Fin 3) α` (see also `Matrix.row`).
* `!![a; b; c]` is a column vector of type `Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 1) α` (see also `Matrix.col`).

This notation implements some special cases:

* `![,,]`, with `n` `,`s, is a term of type `Matrix (Fin 0) (Fin n) α`
* `![;;]`, with `m` `;`s, is a term of type `Matrix (Fin m) (Fin 0) α`
* `![]` is the 0×0 matrix

Note that vector notation is provided elsewhere (by `Matrix.vecNotation`) as `![a, b, c]`.
Under the hood, `!![a, b, c; d, e, f]` is syntax for `Matrix.of ![![a, b, c], ![d, e, f]]`.

  {n₂ : Type u_7} [Fintype n] [Fintype n₁] [Fintype n₂] [DecidableEq n] [DecidableEq n₁] [DecidableEq n₂] [CommRing R]
  (e : n ≃ n₁ ⊕ n₂) (A₁ : Matrix n n₁ R) (A₂ : Matrix n n₂ R) (B₁ : Matrix n₁ n R) (B₂ : Matrix n₂ n R) :
  A₁.fromColumns A₂ * B₁.fromRows B₂ = 1 ↔ B₁.fromRows B₂ * A₁.fromColumns A₂ = 1
Matrix.fromColumns_mul_fromRows_eq_one_c.comment:
Multiplication of a matrix by its inverse is commutative.
This is the column and row partitioned matrix form of `Matrix.mul_eq_one_comm`.

The condition `e : n ≃ n₁ ⊕ n₂` states that `fromColumns A₁ A₂` and `fromRows B₁ B₂` are "square".

Computation.comment:
`Computation α` is the type of unbounded computations returning `α`.
An element of `Computation α` is an infinite sequence of `Option α` such
that if `f n = some a` for some `n` then it is constantly `some a` after that.

explanatories.Option.some: The statement defines a constructor that produces an option type containing a specified value of a given type.

Computation.fullDefinition: def Computation (α : Type u) : Type u :=   { f : Stream' (Option α) // ∀ ⦃n a⦄, f n = some a → f (n + 1) = some a }
Computation.description: The type of computations returning a value consists of infinite sequences of optional values that, once a value is produced, continue to yield that value indefinitely.

Computation.pure.code: Computation.pure.{u} {α : Type u} (a : α) : Computation α
Computation.pure.comment: `pure a` is the computation that immediately terminates with result `a`.

explanatories.Option.some: The statement defines a constructor that produces an option type containing a specified value of a given type.
explanatories.Pure.pure: The operation produces a monadic action that encapsulates a given value without altering it.

Computation.pure.fullDefinition: def pure (a : α) : Computation α :=   ⟨Stream'.const (some a), fun _ _ => id⟩
Computation.pure.description: The computation that immediately provides a specified value without any delay is defined as 'pure'.

Computation.think.code: Computation.think.{u} {α : Type u} (c : Computation α) : Computation α
Computation.think.comment:
`think c` is the computation that delays for one "tick" and then performs
computation `c`.

explanatories.Option.none: The representation of an absence of value in an option type is denoted by "none."
explanatories.List.cons: This creates a new list by adding a specified element to the front of an existing list.

Computation.think.fullDefinition: def think (c : Computation α) : Computation α :=   ⟨Stream'.cons none c.1, fun n a h => by     cases' n with n     · contradiction     · exact c.2 h⟩
Computation.think.description: The computation that introduces a delay for one unit of time before proceeding with another computation is defined as 'think'.

Computation.thinkN.code: Computation.thinkN.{u} {α : Type u} (c : Computation α) : ℕ → Computation α
Computation.thinkN.comment:
`thinkN c n` is the computation that delays for `n` ticks and then performs
computation `c`.

explanatories.Bool.false: The value `false` represents one of the two possible truth values in Boolean logic.

Computation.thinkN.fullDefinition: def thinkN (c : Computation α) : ℕ → Computation α   | 0 => c   | n + 1 => think (thinkN c n) set_option linter.uppercaseLean3 false in
Computation.thinkN.description: The computation that introduces a delay of a specified number of time units before proceeding with another computation is defined as 'thinkN'.

Computation.head.code: Computation.head.{u} {α : Type u} (c : Computation α) : Option α
Computation.head.comment:
`head c` is the first step of computation, either `some a` if `c = pure a`
or `none` if `c = think c'`.
Computation.head.fullDefinition: def head (c : Computation α) : Option α :=   c.1.head
Computation.head.description: The function retrieves the first result of a computation, yielding either an optional value if it completes immediately or nothing if it is still processing.

Computation.tail.code: Computation.tail.{u} {α : Type u} (c : Computation α) : Computation α
Computation.tail.comment:
`tail c` is the remainder of computation, either `c` if `c = pure a`
or `c'` if `c = think c'`.
Computation.tail.fullDefinition: def tail (c : Computation α) : Computation α :=   ⟨c.1.tail, fun _ _ h => c.2 h⟩
Computation.tail.description: The operation that retrieves the remaining part of a computation, distinguishing between an immediate result and a delayed computation, is defined as 'tail'.

Computation.empty.comment:
`empty α` is the computation that never returns, an infinite sequence of
`think`s.

explanatories.Option.none: The representation of an absence of value in an option type is denoted by "none."

Computation.empty.fullDefinition: def empty (α) : Computation α :=   ⟨Stream'.const none, fun _ _ => id⟩
Computation.empty.description: The computation defined as 'empty' represents an eternal delay, resulting in a sequence that never produces a value.

Computation.runFor.code: Computation.runFor.{u} {α : Type u} : Computation α → ℕ → Option α
Computation.runFor.comment:
`runFor c n` evaluates `c` for `n` steps and returns the result, or `none`
if it did not terminate after `n` steps.
Computation.runFor.fullDefinition: def runFor : Computation α → ℕ → Option α :=   Subtype.val
Computation.runFor.description: The function evaluates a computation for a specified number of steps, returning the result if it completes or indicating failure if it does not terminate within that limit.

Computation.destruct.code: Computation.destruct.{u} {α : Type u} (c : Computation α) : α ⊕ Computation α
Computation.destruct.comment:
`destruct c` is the destructor for `Computation α` as a coinductive type.
It returns `inl a` if `c = pure a` and `inr c'` if `c = think c'`.

explanatories.Option.none: The representation of an absence of value in an option type is denoted by "none."

explanatories.Sum.inl: The left injection function creates a sum type by embedding an element from the first type into a union of two types.
explanatories.Or.inl: The left injection into a disjunction allows a proven statement to be included as a true proposition within either of the options of an "or" logical construction.
explanatories.Or.inr: The right injection operation allows one to obtain a disjunction by confirming the truth of a specific proposition.

Computation.destruct.fullDefinition: def destruct (c : Computation α) : Sum α (Computation α) :=   match c.1 0 with   | none => Sum.inr (tail c)   | some a => Sum.inl a
Computation.destruct.description: The destructor for a computation type produces either a value if the computation is complete or a new computation if it is still processing.

Computation.run.code: Computation.run.{u} {α : Type u} : Computation α → α
Computation.run.comment:
`run c` is an unsound meta function that runs `c` to completion, possibly
resulting in an infinite loop in the VM.

Computation.recOn.fullDefinition: def recOn {C : Computation α → Sort v} (s : Computation α) (h1 : ∀ a, C (pure a))     (h2 : ∀ s, C (think s)) : C s :=   match H : destruct s with   | Sum.inl v => by     rw [destruct_eq_pure H]     apply h1   | Sum.inr v => match v with     | ⟨a, s'⟩ => by       rw [destruct_eq_think H]       apply h2
Computation.recOn.description: The recursion principle for computation types allows one to define a property for all computations by specifying how it applies to immediate results and delayed computations.

Computation.Corec.f.fullDefinition: def Corec.f (f : β → Sum α β) : Sum α β → Option α × Sum α β   | Sum.inl a => (some a, Sum.inl a)   | Sum.inr b =>     (match f b with       | Sum.inl a => some a       | Sum.inr _ => none,       f b) set_option linter.uppercaseLean3 false in

Computation.corec.code: Computation.corec.{u, v} {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (f : β → α ⊕ β) (b : β) : Computation α
Computation.corec.comment:
`corec f b` is the corecursor for `Computation α` as a coinductive type.
If `f b = inl a` then `corec f b = pure a`, and if `f b = inl b'` then
`corec f b = think (corec f b')`.

Computation.corec.fullDefinition: def corec (f : β → Sum α β) (b : β) : Computation α := by   refine ⟨Stream'.corec' (Corec.f f) (Sum.inr b), fun n a' h => ?_⟩   rw [Stream'.corec'_eq]   change Stream'.corec' (Corec.f f) (Corec.f f (Sum.inr b)).2 n = some a'   revert h; generalize Sum.inr b = o; revert o   induction' n with n IH <;> intro o   · change (Corec.f f o).1 = some a' → (Corec.f f (Corec.f f o).2).1 = some a'     cases' o with _ b <;> intro h     · exact h     unfold Corec.f at *; split <;> simp_all   · rw [Stream'.corec'_eq (Corec.f f) (Corec.f f o).2, Stream'.corec'_eq (Corec.f f) o]     exact IH (Corec.f f o).2
Computation.corec.description: The corec function defines a coinductive computation based on a function and an initial value, producing results according to the specified cases of that function.

Computation.LiftRel.comment:
`LiftRel R ca cb` is a generalization of `Equiv` to relations other than
equality. It asserts that if `ca` terminates with `a`, then `cb` terminates with
some `b` such that `R a b`, and if `cb` terminates with `b` then `ca` terminates
with some `a` such that `R a b`.

Computation.LiftRel.fullDefinition: def LiftRel (R : α → β → Prop) (ca : Computation α) (cb : Computation β) : Prop :=   (∀ {a}, a ∈ ca → ∃ b, b ∈ cb ∧ R a b) ∧ ∀ {b}, b ∈ cb → ∃ a, a ∈ ca ∧ R a b
Computation.LiftRel.description: The defined relation generalizes the equivalence concept, asserting that the termination of one computation guarantees a corresponding termination in another, adhering to a specified relation between their results.

Stream'.WSeq.comment:
Weak sequences.

While the `Seq` structure allows for lists which may not be finite,
a weak sequence also allows the computation of each element to
involve an indeterminate amount of computation, including possibly
an infinite loop. This is represented as a regular `Seq` interspersed
with `none` elements to indicate that computation is ongoing.

This model is appropriate for Haskell style lazy lists, and is closed
under most interesting computation patterns on infinite lists,
but conversely it is difficult to extract elements from it.
Stream'.WSeq.description: This defines a structure for weak sequences that can include indefinite computations represented by `none` elements amid regular sequences.

Computation.parallelRec.fullDefinition: def parallelRec {S : WSeq (Computation α)} (C : α → Sort v) (H : ∀ s ∈ S, ∀ a ∈ s, C a) {a}     (h : a ∈ parallel S) : C a := by   let T : WSeq (Computation (α × Computation α)) := S.map fun c => c.map fun a => (a, c)   have : S = T.map (map fun c => c.1) := by     rw [← WSeq.map_comp]     refine (WSeq.map_id _).symm.trans (congr_arg (fun f => WSeq.map f S) ?_)     funext c     dsimp [id, Function.comp_def]     rw [← map_comp]     exact (map_id _).symm   have pe := congr_arg parallel this   rw [← map_parallel] at pe   have h' := h   rw [pe] at h'   haveI : Terminates (parallel T) := (terminates_map_iff _ _).1 ⟨⟨_, h'⟩⟩   induction' e : get (parallel T) with a' c   have : a ∈ c ∧ c ∈ S := by     rcases exists_of_mem_map h' with ⟨d, dT, cd⟩     rw [get_eq_of_mem _ dT] at e     cases e     dsimp at cd     cases cd     rcases exists_of_mem_parallel dT with ⟨d', dT', ad'⟩     rcases WSeq.exists_of_mem_map dT' with ⟨c', cs', e'⟩     rw [← e'] at ad'     rcases exists_of_mem_map ad' with ⟨a', ac', e'⟩     injection e' with i1 i2     constructor     · rwa [i1, i2] at ac'     · rwa [i2] at cs'   cases' this with ac cs   apply H _ cs _ ac

PosNum.minFacAux.comment:
Auxiliary function for computing the smallest prime factor of a `PosNum`. Unlike
`Nat.minFacAux`, we use a natural number `fuel` variable that is set to an upper bound on the
number of iterations. It is initialized to the number `n` we are determining primality for. Even
though this is exponential in the input (since it is a `Nat`, not a `Num`), it will get lazily
evaluated during kernel reduction, so we will only require about `sqrt n` unfoldings, for the
`sqrt n` iterations of the loop.

Ordnode.delta.comment:
**Internal use only**

The maximal relative difference between the sizes of
two trees, it corresponds with the `w` in Adams' paper.

According to the Haskell comment, only `(delta, ratio)` settings
of `(3, 2)` and `(4, 2)` will work, and the proofs in
`Ordset.lean` assume `delta := 3` and `ratio := 2`.

Ordnode.ratio.comment:
**Internal use only**

The ratio between an outer and inner sibling of the
heavier subtree in an unbalanced setting. It determines
whether a double or single rotation should be performed
to restore balance. It is corresponds with the inverse
of `α` in Adam's article.

symmetries in the algorithms.

Ordnode.Amem.code: Ordnode.Amem.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [LE α] (x : α) : Ordnode α → Prop
Ordnode.Amem.comment:
O(n). Approximate membership in the set, that is, whether some element in the
set is equivalent to this one in the preorder. This is useful primarily for stating
correctness properties; use `∈` for a version that actually uses the BST property
of the tree.

    Amem 2 {1, 2, 3} = true
    Amem 4 {1, 2, 3} = false

To see the difference with `Emem`, we need a preorder that is not a partial order.
For example, suppose we compare pairs of numbers using only their first coordinate. Then:
-- Porting note: Verify below example
    emem (0, 1) {(0, 0), (1, 2)} = false
    amem (0, 1) {(0, 0), (1, 2)} = true
    (0, 1) ∈ {(0, 0), (1, 2)} = true

The `∈` relation is equivalent to `Amem` as long as the `Ordnode` is well formed,
and should always be used instead of `Amem`.

Ordnode.link.fullDefinition: def link (l : Ordnode α) (x : α) : Ordnode α → Ordnode α :=   -- Porting note: Previous code was:   -- (Ordnode.recOn l (insertMin x)) fun ls ll lx lr IHll IHlr r =>   --   (Ordnode.recOn r (insertMax l x)) fun rs rl rx rr IHrl IHrr =>   --     if delta * ls < rs then balanceL IHrl rx rr   --     else if delta * rs < ls then balanceR ll lx (IHlr r) else node' l x r   --   -- failed to elaborate eliminator, expected type is not available.   match l with   | nil => insertMin x   | node ls ll lx lr => fun r ↦     match r with     | nil => insertMax l x     | node rs rl rx rr =>       if delta * ls < rs then balanceL (link ll x rl) rx rr       else if delta * rs < ls then balanceR ll lx (link lr x rr)       else node' l x r

Ordnode.ofAscListAux₁.comment:
Auxiliary definition for `ofAscList`.

**Note:** This function is defined by well founded recursion, so it will probably not compute
in the kernel, meaning that you probably can't prove things like
`ofAscList [1, 2, 3] = {1, 2, 3}` by `rfl`.
This implementation is optimized for VM evaluation.

Ordnode.ofAscListAux₁.fullDefinition: def ofAscListAux₁ : ∀ l : List α, ℕ → Ordnode α × { l' : List α // l'.length ≤ l.length }   | [] => fun _ => (nil, ⟨[], le_rfl⟩)   | x :: xs => fun s =>     if s = 1 then (ι x, ⟨xs, Nat.le_succ _⟩)     else       match ofAscListAux₁ xs (s <<< 1) with       | (t, ⟨[], _⟩) => (t, ⟨[], Nat.zero_le _⟩)       | (l, ⟨y :: ys, h⟩) =>         have := Nat.le_succ_of_le h         let (r, ⟨zs, h'⟩) := ofAscListAux₁ ys (s <<< 1)         (link l y r, ⟨zs, le_trans h' (le_of_lt this)⟩)         termination_by l => l.length

Ordnode.mem.code: Ordnode.mem.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [LE α] [DecidableRel fun x x_1 => x ≤ x_1] (x : α) : Ordnode α → Bool
Ordnode.mem.comment:
O(log n). Does the set (approximately) contain the element `x`? That is,
is there an element that is equivalent to `x` in the order?

    1 ∈ {1, 2, 3} = true
    4 ∈ {1, 2, 3} = false

Using a preorder on `ℕ × ℕ` that only compares the first coordinate:

    (1, 1) ∈ {(0, 1), (1, 2)} = true
    (3, 1) ∈ {(0, 1), (1, 2)} = false

  Ordnode α → Ordnode α × Ordnode α
Ordnode.split.comment:
O(log n). Split the tree into those smaller than `x` and those greater than it.
If an element equivalent to `x` is in the set, it is discarded.

    split 2 {1, 2, 4} = ({1}, {4})
    split 3 {1, 2, 4} = ({1, 2}, {4})
    split 4 {1, 2, 4} = ({1, 2}, ∅)

Using a preorder on `ℕ × ℕ` that only compares the first coordinate:

    split (1, 1) {(0, 1), (1, 2)} = ({(0, 1)}, ∅)
    split (3, 1) {(0, 1), (1, 2)} = ({(0, 1), (1, 2)}, ∅)

  (ind :

          { s := s₁, i := i₁ }.hasNext = true →
            s₁.get i₁ = s₂.get i₂ →
              motive { s := s₁, i := i₁ }.next { s := s₂, i := i₂ }.next →
                motive { s := s₁, i := i₁ } { s := s₂, i := i₂ })
  (eq :

      (i₁ i₂ : Pos) →
        { s := s₂, i := i₂ }.hasNext = true →
          { s := s₁, i := i₁ }.hasNext = true →
            ¬s₁.get i₁ = s₂.get i₂ → motive { s := s₁, i := i₁ } { s := s₂, i := i₂ })
  (base₁ :
    (s₁ s₂ : String) →
      (i₁ i₂ : Pos) →
        { s := s₂, i := i₂ }.hasNext = true →
          ¬{ s := s₁, i := i₁ }.hasNext = true → motive { s := s₁, i := i₁ } { s := s₂, i := i₂ })
  (base₂ :
    (s₁ s₂ : String) →
      (i₁ i₂ : Pos) → ¬{ s := s₂, i := i₂ }.hasNext = true → motive { s := s₁, i := i₁ } { s := s₂, i := i₂ }) :
  motive it₁ it₂

Fin.contractNth.fullDefinition: def contractNth (j : Fin (n + 1)) (op : α → α → α) (g : Fin (n + 1) → α) (k : Fin n) : α :=   if (k : ℕ) < j then g (Fin.castSucc k)   else if (k : ℕ) = j then op (g (Fin.castSucc k)) (g k.succ) else g k.succ

Fin.contractNth_apply_of_lt.description: This theorem demonstrates that contracting a specific position in a function using a binary operation results in the same value as applying the function at a modified index, provided that the index is less than the position being contracted.

Tuple.eq_sort_iff.code:
Tuple.eq_sort_iff.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {α : Type u_1} [LinearOrder α] {f : Fin n → α} {σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)} :
  σ = sort f ↔ Monotone (f ∘ ⇑σ) ∧ ∀ (i j : Fin n), i < j → f (σ i) = f (σ j) → σ i < σ j
Tuple.eq_sort_iff.comment:
A permutation `σ` equals `sort f` if and only if `f ∘ σ` is monotone and whenever `i < j`
and `f (σ i) = f (σ j)`, then `σ i < σ j`. This means that `sort f` is the lexicographically
smallest permutation `σ` such that `f ∘ σ` is monotone.

Tuple.bubble_sort_induction'.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {α : Type u_1} [LinearOrder α] {f : Fin n → α} {P : (Fin n → α) → Prop}
  (hf : P f)
  (h :
    ∀ (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (i j : Fin n),
      i < j → (f ∘ ⇑σ) j < (f ∘ ⇑σ) i → P (f ∘ ⇑σ) → P (f ∘ ⇑σ ∘ ⇑(Equiv.swap i j))) :
  P (f ∘ ⇑(sort f))
Tuple.bubble_sort_induction'.comment:
*Bubble sort induction*: Prove that the sorted version of `f` has some property `P`
if `f` satisfies `P` and `P` is preserved on permutations of `f` when swapping two
antitone values.

List.Nat.antidiagonalTuple.code: List.Nat.antidiagonalTuple (k : ℕ) : ℕ → List (Fin k → ℕ)
List.Nat.antidiagonalTuple.comment:
`List.antidiagonalTuple k n` is a list of all `k`-tuples which sum to `n`.

This list contains no duplicates (`List.Nat.nodup_antidiagonalTuple`), and is sorted
lexicographically (`List.Nat.antidiagonalTuple_pairwise_pi_lex`), starting with `![0, ..., n]`
and ending with `![n, ..., 0]`.

```
#eval antidiagonalTuple 3 2
-- [![0, 0, 2], ![0, 1, 1], ![0, 2, 0], ![1, 0, 1], ![1, 1, 0], ![2, 0, 0]]
```

explanatories.Multiset.map: This definition outlines a way to create a new multiset by applying a function to each element of an existing multiset, preserving the count of each element according to how many times the function produces the same output.
explanatories.Finset.HasAntidiagonal.antidiagonal: This definition describes the antidiagonal of an element as the set of pairs of elements that sum up to that element.
explanatories.Finset.map: This definition specifies a function that transforms a finite set by mapping its elements through an injective function, ensuring that the resulting set has no duplicates.

Finset.Nat.sigmaAntidiagonalTupleEquivTu.code: Finset.Nat.sigmaAntidiagonalTupleEquivTuple (k : ℕ) : (n : ℕ) × { x // x ∈ antidiagonalTuple k n } ≃ (Fin k → ℕ)
Finset.Nat.sigmaAntidiagonalTupleEquivTu.comment:
The disjoint union of antidiagonal tuples `Σ n, antidiagonalTuple k n` is equivalent to the
`k`-tuple `Fin k → ℕ`. This is such an equivalence, obtained by mapping `(n, x)` to `x`.

This is the tuple version of `Finset.sigmaAntidiagonalEquivProd`.

Matrix.vecCons.comment:
`vecCons h t` prepends an entry `h` to a vector `t`.

The notation `![a, b, ...]` expands to `vecCons a (vecCons b ...)`.

Matrix.vecNotation.comment:
`![...]` notation is used to construct a vector `Fin n → α` using `Matrix.vecEmpty` and
`Matrix.vecCons`.

For instance, `![a, b, c] : Fin 3` is syntax for `vecCons a (vecCons b (vecCons c vecEmpty))`.

Note that this should not be used as syntax for `Matrix` as it generates a term with the wrong type.
The `!![a, b; c, d]` syntax (provided by `Matrix.matrixNotation`) should be used instead.

PiFin.toExpr.fullDefinition: protected instance _root_.PiFin.toExpr [ToLevel.{u}] [ToExpr α] (n : ℕ) : ToExpr (Fin n → α) :=   have lu := toLevel.{u}   have eα : Q(Type $lu) := toTypeExpr α   have toTypeExpr := q(Fin $n → $eα)   match n with   | 0 => { toTypeExpr, toExpr := fun _ => q(@vecEmpty $eα) }   | n + 1 =>     { toTypeExpr, toExpr := fun v =>       have := PiFin.toExpr n       have eh : Q($eα) := toExpr (vecHead v)       have et : Q(Fin $n → $eα) := toExpr (vecTail v)       q(vecCons $eh $et) }
PiFin.toExpr.description: This definition introduces a function that converts a finite function indexed by natural numbers into an expression suitable for Lean's type system.

Matrix.vecAppend.code: Matrix.vecAppend.{u_4} {m n : ℕ} {α : Type u_4} {o : ℕ} (ho : o = m + n) (u : Fin m → α) (v : Fin n → α) : Fin o → α
Matrix.vecAppend.comment:
`vecAppend ho u v` appends two vectors of lengths `m` and `n` to produce
one of length `o = m + n`. This is a variant of `Fin.append` with an additional `ho` argument,
which provides control of definitional equality for the vector length.

This turns out to be helpful when providing simp lemmas to reduce `![a, b, c] n`, and also means
that `vecAppend ho u v 0` is valid. `Fin.append u v 0` is not valid in this case because there is
no `Zero (Fin (m + n))` instance.

Matrix.vecAppend.fullDefinition: def vecAppend {α : Type*} {o : ℕ} (ho : o = m + n) (u : Fin m → α) (v : Fin n → α) : Fin o → α :=   Fin.append u v ∘ Fin.cast ho
Matrix.vecAppend.description: This definition describes a function that combines two vectors of specified lengths into a single vector of the total length, ensuring that the lengths are compatible through an additional parameter for definitional equality.

explanatories.ContravariantClass.mk: This theorem illustrates how a property of contravariance can be constructed from a specified action and relation, effectively creating a class that encapsulates those characteristics.
explanatories.IsWellFounded.mk: A theorem establishing that if a relation is well-founded, then it is also well-founded in the context of the specified type.
explanatories.Subtype.mk: This constructs a subtype from a value and a property that the value satisfies.
explanatories.Sub.mk: This constructs a subtype that contains elements satisfying a certain binary operation on a given type.
explanatories.Union.mk: This theorem defines a procedure to construct a union type from a given binary operation on elements of a specified type.
explanatories.Inter.mk: This theorem describes a function that takes an intersection operation on a type and produces a new structure representing the intersection of that type.

explanatories.DecidableEq: A type with decidable equality allows for determining whether any two elements are equal or not.

explanatories.Subtype.eq: This theorem states that if two subtypes of a type are equal as sets, then the underlying elements of those subtypes are also equal.

Multiset.rec.fullDefinition: def rec (C_0 : C 0) (C_cons : ∀ a m, C m → C (a ::ₘ m))     (C_cons_heq :       ∀ a a' m b, HEq (C_cons a (a' ::ₘ m) (C_cons a' m b)) (C_cons a' (a ::ₘ m) (C_cons a m b)))     (m : Multiset α) : C m :=   Quotient.hrecOn m (@List.rec α (fun l => C ⟦l⟧) C_0 fun a l b => C_cons a ⟦l⟧ b) fun l l' h =>     h.rec_heq       (fun hl _ ↦ by congr 1; exact Quot.sound hl)       (C_cons_heq _ _ ⟦_⟧ _)
Multiset.rec.description: This definition establishes a method for recursively constructing a property for multisets based on a base case for the empty multiset and an inductive case for adding elements, while also including a condition to ensure the consistency of the induction process.

Multiset.Subset.comment:
`s ⊆ t` is the lift of the list subset relation. It means that any
element with nonzero multiplicity in `s` has nonzero multiplicity in `t`,
but it does not imply that the multiplicity of `a` in `s` is less or equal than in `t`;
see `s ≤ t` for this relation.

Multiset.subset_iff.description: This theorem states that a multiset is a subset of another multiset if and only if every element of the first multiset is also an element of the second multiset.

Multiset.mem_of_subset.code: Multiset.mem_of_subset.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s t : Multiset α} {a : α} (h : s ⊆ t) : a ∈ s → a ∈ t
Multiset.mem_of_subset.description: This theorem states that if one multiset is a subset of another, then any element belonging to the first multiset must also belong to the second multiset.

Multiset.zero_subset.code: Multiset.zero_subset.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (s : Multiset α) : 0 ⊆ s
Multiset.zero_subset.description: This theorem states that the empty multiset is a subset of any multiset.

Multiset.subset_cons.code: Multiset.subset_cons.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (s : Multiset α) (a : α) : s ⊆ a ::ₘ s
Multiset.subset_cons.description: This theorem asserts that any multiset is a subset of the multiset formed by adding an element to the front of it.

Multiset.ssubset_cons.code: Multiset.ssubset_cons.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s : Multiset α} {a : α} (ha : a ∉ s) : s ⊂ a ::ₘ s
Multiset.ssubset_cons.description: This theorem states that if an element is not in a multiset, then that multiset is a strict subset of the multiset formed by adding that element to it.

Multiset.cons_subset.code: Multiset.cons_subset.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {a : α} {s t : Multiset α} : a ::ₘ s ⊆ t ↔ a ∈ t ∧ s ⊆ t
Multiset.cons_subset.description: This theorem states that a multiset formed by adding an element to another multiset is a subset of a third multiset if and only if the added element is contained in the third multiset and the second multiset is a subset of the third.

Multiset.cons_subset_cons.code: Multiset.cons_subset_cons.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {a : α} {s t : Multiset α} : s ⊆ t → a ::ₘ s ⊆ a ::ₘ t
Multiset.cons_subset_cons.description: This theorem asserts that if one multiset is a subset of another, then adding the same element to both multisets preserves the subset relationship.

Multiset.eq_zero_of_subset_zero.code: Multiset.eq_zero_of_subset_zero.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s : Multiset α} (h : s ⊆ 0) : s = 0
Multiset.eq_zero_of_subset_zero.description: This theorem states that if a multiset is a subset of the empty multiset, then it must itself be empty.

Multiset.subset_zero.code: Multiset.subset_zero.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {s : Multiset α} : s ⊆ 0 ↔ s = 0
Multiset.subset_zero.description: This theorem states that a multiset is a subset of the empty multiset if and only if it is itself empty.
